docs.title: SolidarityNode
docs.text:
Open-source spatial probabilistic framework for social service accessibility, hidden need (κρυφή ανάγκη), vulnerability (τρωτότητα) and resilience (ανθεκτικότητα).

Early development: diagnostic model only

Platform version 0.1.0. The platform works end to end on synthetic data, but the only model is the diagnostic model diagnostic-v0, which checks the platform's mechanics. There are no research results yet. The methods of the four papers are added in order (roadmap).

docs.title: What SolidarityNode is
docs.text:
SolidarityNode is an open-source platform that moves the analysis of social infrastructure (healthcare facilities, social care and other public services) from a static map of spatial adequacy to a dynamic, probabilistic view.

It combines in a single framework:

  • spatial accessibility and capacity of service facilities,
  • estimation of hidden social need: need that is never expressed as a request,
  • vulnerability of population groups: how a service disruption turns into consequences for each group,
  • real operational data from the services themselves (anonymous request tickets),
  • the dynamics of impact and recovery over time, leading to estimates of system resilience.

A degraded facility is not automatically treated as lost service. The platform estimates what the population of each area actually loses, given the alternative facilities and routes available in the network, and how the system recovers after a disruption.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
The framework is developed in four connected parts (see the domain model):

flowchart LR
    P1["1. Accessibility, capacity,<br/>demand, service gap"] --> P2["2. Social susceptibility,<br/>hidden need, total need"]
    P1 --> P3
    P2 --> P3["3. Disruption scenarios, exposure,<br/>service loss, vulnerability"]
    P3 --> P4["4. Operations, dynamics,<br/>recovery, resilience"]
    OPS[("Anonymous request<br/>tickets")] --> P4
  1. Baseline: group-specific accessibility, facility capacity shared among the areas that reach it (two-step floating catchment area), estimated demand and the service gap.
  2. Hidden need: total need is the share of a group that needs a service; a latent non-take-up level, informed by social susceptibility, the shortfall of supply against total need, access deterrence and alternatives outside the network, splits it into visible and hidden need.
  3. Vulnerability: simulated disruption scenarios give group exposure and service loss; together with social susceptibility they feed the vulnerability relationship of each group.
  4. Resilience: operational data, the functional state of facilities and areas, and a Dynamic Bayesian Network describe loss and recovery over time; the vulnerability relationship is updated from real observations and resilience is derived from recovery trajectories.

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text:
Unit of analysis. Everything is modelled at the level of:

spatial unit × social group × service × time

Vulnerability is not resilience. The vulnerability of a group is the relationship that turns a disruption into consequences for that group, given its exposure, the service loss and its social susceptibility. A vulnerability value is that relationship evaluated at a given scenario, and maps compare areas at the same standardised reference scenarios (minor, moderate, severe). Resilience is a dynamic property that emerges from the trajectory of loss and recovery. They are modelled separately, and neither is the same as risk.

Facility state is not population-level service loss. A facility can be degraded without any loss of coverage for an area, if alternative facilities and routes still serve it. Coverage is therefore computed at the level of the service network, not the individual facility.

Observed demand is not need. Need is split into three kinds that never overlap: hidden need (never expressed as a request, because people do not seek the service, cannot reach it, are discouraged or use alternatives), unmet expressed need (requests not fulfilled within the service's maximum acceptable waiting time) and met need. Hidden need is estimated explicitly, as a share of the group with an interval.

Social group is not social susceptibility. The group says who is examined; social susceptibility is how prone that group is to unmet provision of a service, from its social characteristics and independently of the service system.

Need is measured in service units. Need, capacity, supply, gap and loss are measured in service units (visits, appointments or hours) per reference period, defined per service. Quantities of different services are never added together.

Uncertainty is first-class. Methods are probabilistic (Bayesian Networks, Dynamic Bayesian Networks and Monte Carlo simulation) so that results carry uncertainty instead of single deterministic numbers. Expert-elicited relationships act as priors, and their parameters are learned as real operational observations accumulate.

Operational support is a system response. Mobilising extra resources (including approved volunteers) is part of how the system responds to a disruption, not an independent measure of resilience.

docs.title: What the platform offers
docs.text: Version 0.1 delivers the platform foundation (A) on synthetic data, without the hub. The analytical tools (B) are added through the tickets of the four papers; the roadmap gives the order and the Kintsugi board the live state.

docs.title: A. Platform foundation
docs.text: The foundation provides the map, scenarios, runs and data management that the analytical tools later plug into.

docs.title: Users and roles
docs.text:
• Sign-in with an account.
  • Roles: admin (users, data), analyst (scenarios, runs), viewer (sees shared work).

docs.title: Study area on a map
docs.text:
• Spatial units, facilities and the road network of one or more municipalities, plus a buffer of neighbouring areas, so that people served across the boundary are counted correctly.
  • A quality flag on every feature (open data, estimate, verified by the municipality) and an edge-effect warning where data on neighbours is missing.

docs.title: "What if…" scenarios
docs.text:
• Built by clicking on the map: increase or reduce capacity, add a facility, degrade or close a facility, close a road.
  • Every change is kept as a version. Scenarios are private or shared.

docs.title: Runs
docs.text:
• Run in the background, with progress and cancellation.
  • Every run is fully reproducible: it records the data version, code, model, parameters and random seed.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Maps and tables by spatial unit, social group and service, with uncertainty always visible.
  • Comparison with the current situation (side by side or a difference map).
  • Export to CSV and GeoPackage, together with the reproducibility details.

docs.title: Data and updates
docs.text:
• Import of data packages with integrity checks and a preview of changes before they are applied.
  • Past results never change. Scenarios can be rerun on new data and compared.

docs.title: Central hub (planned: v0.2, hub onboarding)
docs.text:
• Registration of national sources (boundaries, network, population) without processing the whole country.
  • Step-by-step onboarding of a municipality, with a coverage matrix showing what is available and what is missing.
  • Import and extension of facilities from Excel, CSV or GeoPackage, with an error report and change history.
  • Publication of packages per municipality, and a notice when onboarding a neighbour improves another municipality's data.

docs.title: B. Analytical tools
docs.text: Each paper adds an analytical tool on top of the foundation, in the order 1 → 2 → 3 → 4.

docs.title: Accessibility and adequacy (Paper 1)
docs.text:
• Travel times by group and transport mode (walking, car, public transport).
  • Actual service supply per area, taking into account that several areas share the same facilities.
  • Service gap by group, with an explanation of why (low capacity, poor access or high demand).

docs.title: Hidden need (Paper 2)
docs.text:
• Estimate of the share of each group with need that is not visible, for example "7–17 % of older people in local community X".
  • A map of areas where recorded demand most likely underestimates reality.

docs.title: Vulnerability (Paper 3)
docs.text:
• What each group loses when a facility is degraded or closed, or a road is cut, taking alternatives into account.
  • Maps at standard reference scenarios (minor, moderate, severe disruption), so that areas are compared fairly.
  • How many people are affected and how deeply, not only how much service is lost overall.

docs.title: Real operation and resilience (Paper 4)
docs.text:
• Anonymous request logging (QR code or appointments) at facilities, with no personal data.
  • Operational indicators: waiting time, delay, unmet requests, coverage.
  • State of each facility (normal, under pressure, degraded, critical, recovering) and an operational view: "which facility needs help now, and of what kind".
  • Monitoring of recovery after a disruption and estimation of resilience by spatial unit, group and service.
  • Estimates learn from real operation over time.

docs.title: Shared tools
docs.text:
• Uncertainty analysis (Monte Carlo) and sensitivity analysis ("which factor matters most").
  • Expert elicitation tools that feed the probabilistic models.

docs.title: C. Principles that apply everywhere
docs.text:
• Open source, with no closed editions.
  • Privacy by design: no personal data. Operational data stays with the municipality; only anonymous aggregates are shared upwards, and only if the municipality chooses to.
  • One installation per municipality, or group of municipalities, with a shared hub for open data.
  • Reproducibility: every result can be reproduced exactly.
  • Transparency: every dataset has a source and a processing note, and every method decision is recorded.

docs.title: Open questions at a glance
docs.text:
The method still has open questions; code never resolves them (how they are handled). Current state, counted from the summary table of open-questions.md:

30 questions: 10 decided, 2 partly decided, 1 proposed, 17 open.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: The framework draws on the literature on accessibility (Geurs & van Wee, 2004), social vulnerability (Cutter et al., 2003; Adger, 2006), community and system resilience (Holling, 1973; Bruneau et al., 2003; Norris et al., 2008), critical infrastructure interdependencies (Rinaldi et al., 2001), probabilistic graphical models (Pearl, 1988; Koller & Friedman, 2009; Murphy, 2002) and Digital Twins (Grieves & Vickers, 2017). A full reference list will be added with the per-paper specifications.

docs.text: Status: platform 0.1.0, platform mechanics (no scientific method yet: the only model is the diagnostic model diagnostic-v0). It will grow with each module. The science is specified in docs/specs/; decisions are recorded in docs/adr/.

docs.text:

    core -. never .-x backend

  • backend → core, never the reverse. core must not import backend, frontend, any web framework or any database layer.
  • Enforced by core/tests/test_package.py (AST scan of imports and of declared dependencies) and by the ruff banned-api rule in core/pyproject.toml.
  • The frontend talks to the backend only through the HTTP API (frontend/src/api/client.ts).

docs.title: 3. The paper pipeline
docs.text:
The four papers form a pipeline; each core module implements parts of one or more papers (module map: specs/00-domain-model.md §6).

flowchart TB
    subgraph P1["Paper 1: baseline"]
        ACC[accessibility] --> CAP["capacity<br/>2SFCA, OQ-2"]
        DEM[demand] --> SG[service_gap]
        CAP --> SG
    end
    subgraph P2["Paper 2: hidden need"]
        SS["Social Susceptibility<br/>SS_i,g,s"] --> NTU["non-take-up level<br/>(latent)"]
        NBG[need-based gap] --> NTU
        AD[access deterrence] --> NTU
        ALT[outside alternatives] --> NTU
        NTU --> ETN["Estimated Total Need<br/>Population × p × k"]
    end
    subgraph P3["Paper 3: disruption and vulnerability"]
        SCN["scenarios<br/>DS_f,c, rationing"] --> GE[Group Exposure]
        SCN --> SL["Service Loss<br/>ΔPUN / ETN"]
        GE --> V["vulnerability relationship<br/>P(V | GE, SL, SS)"]
        SL --> V
    end
    subgraph P4["Paper 4: operations, dynamics, resilience"]
        TIX[(anonymous tickets)] --> OPS["operations<br/>indicators, facility state"]
        OPS --> DYN["dynamics<br/>territorial state, DBN"]
        DYN --> OBS["observed GE(t), SL(t)"]
        OBS --> EXP[expected consequence]
        DYN --> TRJ[recovery trajectory]
        TRJ --> RES[resilience]
        EXP --> UPD["parameter learning<br/>of P(V | GE, SL, SS)"]
    end
    CAP -->|supply| NBG
    ACC --> AD
    SS --> V
    ETN --> SL
    CAP --> SL
    V --> EXP
    TIX -. "observed use, take-up learning (OQ-8)" .-> NTU

Cross-cutting modules used by all papers: model, bayes, uncertainty (Monte Carlo), sensitivity, validation.

Key separations (AGENTS.md invariants): vulnerability (a relationship, Paper 3) is not resilience (a trajectory property, Paper 4); a facility's state is not a unit's service loss; estimated demand is not need; a social group is not its susceptibility.

docs.title: 4. Ticket data flow
docs.text:
Anonymous request tickets (Paper 4 §4.1) are the only operational data the platform collects.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Person (QR / appointment form)
    participant API as backend /requests (not yet implemented)
    participant DB as PostGIS
    participant J as background job
    participant C as core.operations / dynamics / resilience
    P->>API: unit, group, service, facility (OQ-29), timestamps, first-request flag
    Note over API: schema rejects any other field (no names, contacts, addresses, device ids)
    API->>DB: store ticket (only after ADR 0010 / OQ-21 rules exist)
    J->>DB: read tickets + recording coverage per facility and period
    J->>C: operational indicators, facility state, observed GE(t), SL(t)
    C-->>J: trajectories, updated CPT parameters, resilience
    J->>DB: result index (arrays in Parquet)
  • Privacy rules (minimum cell sizes, retention, aggregation) are open (OQ-21) and must be decided in ADR 0010 before any ticket is stored.
  • Only facilities with full or known recording coverage feed learning (OQ-8).
  • Tickets record the facility where the request is made or scheduled (OQ-29, decided), so indicators, functional state and recording coverage can be computed per facility. The facility field follows the OQ-21 rules.

docs.title: 5. Background jobs and runs
docs.text:
Model runs never execute inside a request handler. The run lifecycle (sequence diagram) and the run statuses (state diagram) are in Lifecycles and data model.

  • Interface: JobRunner (submit(kind, payload), info, cancel) in backend/.../jobs/; implementation PostgresJobRunner; worker python -m solidaritynode_backend.worker (ADR 0006).
  • A stopped worker marks its running job failed. A running job holds a lease (jobs.heartbeat_at, renewed by its worker); any worker fails a job whose lease expired, for example after SIGKILL. An optional maximum runtime per job kind stops a job and marks it failed.
  • Runs record every reproducibility field and an input hash (ADR 0017); models come from the core registry (solidaritynode_core.model.get_registry), which holds only diagnostic-v0.

docs.title: 6. Containers and local development
docs.text:
• make up builds and starts db, backend, worker and frontend with $(COMPOSE) (default podman compose). Docker: CONTAINER_ENGINE=docker COMPOSE="docker compose" make up. ADR 0011.
  • Ports (non-privileged, bound to 127.0.0.1): frontend 8080, backend 8000, database 5432; configurable in .env.
  • The backend container runs alembic upgrade head before starting the API.
  • Database data lives in the named volume db-data, run samples and package uploads in results; there are no bind mounts, so the stack behaves the same under WSL2.
  • make up passes GIT_COMMIT to both image builds; /version and the frontend footer show it with APP_ENV, so a tester knows which build is running. Outside development and test, the backend refuses change-me secrets.
  • make uat resets the database, starts the stack, imports demo package 1.0.0 (which queues the baseline run), seeds the development demo users and prints URLs and credentials; see docs/uat/.

  • Runs record scenario version, package version, git commit, model and parameter version, seed and configuration (ADR 0017).

docs.title: How SolidarityNode works: the main ideas
docs.text: For municipal staff who use the platform: analysts, viewers and administrators. No technical background is needed. Words in bold are the names you see on screen.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
• A data package says what is true: the official data of the study area.
  • A scenario asks what if: a hypothesis on top of that data.
  • A run computes the answer: one scenario on one version of the data, kept unchanged forever.

docs.title: Data package: what is true
docs.text:
A data package holds the official, shared data of the study area: the spatial units and their population by social group, the facilities and the services they offer, and the road network.

  • It is built and published by the hub (the team that prepares data for all municipalities), from official and open sources, with a processing note for every step.
  • It is imported only by an administrator of your installation (Admin → Data packages). Analysts and viewers never upload data.
  • It is versioned: every import creates a new data version (for example 1.0.0, then 1.1.0). Earlier versions are kept, so an administrator can make an earlier one active again.
  • One data version is active: new scenarios and new runs use it.
  • The Study area page shows the active version, its licences, and how good each layer is (verified by the municipality, open data, estimated or missing).

Analysts do not upload data. To try a change, such as a closed road, a new facility or more staff, write a scenario. If the data itself is wrong or out of date (a facility has closed, a real new facility opened, a road number is wrong), send the correction to the hub. It arrives in the next version of the data package, for everyone.

docs.title: Scenario: what if
docs.text:
A scenario is a hypothesis: a list of changes on top of the data. Examples: "road E02 is closed", "facility F3 has one more staff member", "a new community centre opens at node N-B2".

  • A scenario never copies or changes the data; it only describes changes relative to it.
  • It is created against one data version (shown on the scenario page) and checked against it: every facility, road and unit it names must exist.
  • It has an owner and a visibility. Private: visible to its owner and to administrators (administrators run the installation and can see everything). Shared: visible to every user, including viewers.
  • Every save creates a new version of the scenario; earlier versions stay, so runs can always say exactly which version they used.
  • Some changes are recorded only for now (changes to road travel times, new roads, population changes): they are saved and listed, but have no effect on results yet.

docs.title: Run: the answer, kept unchanged
docs.text:
A run is one execution of one scenario version on one data version.

  • It records everything needed to repeat it: scenario and version, data package and version, code version, model and version, random seed and settings.
  • It never changes after it finishes. A new answer always means a new run.
  • Running the same scenario version on the same data with the same settings again does not compute anything: the existing run opens.
  • Results always come with their uncertainty: a central value (the median) and an interval.
  • Until research models are added, results come from a diagnostic model that only checks that the platform works. They are not research results, and every page says so.

docs.title: When the data is updated
docs.text:
When an administrator imports a new data version, or makes an earlier one active again:

  1. A baseline run (no changes) is queued on the new data.
  2. Every scenario is checked again against the new data. A scenario that names something that no longer exists (for example a closed facility) shows Needs attention and cannot run until it is edited.
  3. Existing runs stay as they were: they keep showing the data they used. The run page says "This run used data 1.0.0; the active data is 1.1.0." and offers Rerun on data 1.1.0.
  4. On the scenario page, "Created against data 1.0.0; active data is 1.1.0." reminds you that a new run uses the active data.
  5. In the Scenarios list, a scenario without a run on the active data shows Latest run on data 1.0.0, and a scenario that was never run shows Not run yet.

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text: Role Can Viewer See shared scenarios and their runs: results, map, table, exports. Cannot create, edit or run scenarios; to see results of a scenario that was never run, ask an analyst to run it. Analyst Everything a viewer can, plus create, edit, run, duplicate and share their own scenarios, and run the baseline. Administrator Everything an analyst can, on every scenario (including other users' private ones), plus manage users, import data packages and choose the active data version. Hub (outside your installation) Builds and publishes data packages; receives corrections to the data.

docs.title: Real open data stays local
docs.text:
Open datasets planned for the first application (OpenStreetMap, ELSTAT population, a DEM, GTFS public transport feeds) will be downloaded to data/local/ by scripts in later tickets. data/local/ is git-ignored: nothing in it is ever committed. Each downloaded source gets a row in the table above and each processed dataset a DP-NNN note in docs/data-processing/. No real data has been downloaded yet.

The synthetic demo dataset (data/synthetic/demo/, DP-001) and the demo packages built from it (data/synthetic/packages/, DP-002) use no third-party source.

How to add a source:

  1. Check that the licence allows our use (and redistribution of derived results, if any).
  2. Add a row with the exact attribution text and a link to the licence.
  3. Show the attribution wherever the data is displayed (for example map attributions in the frontend).
  4. Note any share-alike obligations for derived data (for example ODbL for OpenStreetMap).

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: For the maintainer. The version lives in one place, the file VERSION at the repository root.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
SolidarityNode follows semantic versioning. While the version is 0.x:

  • the minor number (0.1.0 → 0.2.0) goes up for new features and for breaking changes (API, scenario schema, data package schema, configuration, database migrations that need care);
  • the patch number (0.1.0 → 0.1.1) goes up for fixes only, with no migration and no change of behaviour beyond the fix;
  • 1.0.0 will mean a stable API and data formats for installations.

VERSION is the single source. make version-sync writes it into core/pyproject.toml, backend/pyproject.toml, frontend/package.json and the uv locks; make lint fails if they differ. From there it reaches /version, the frontend footer, the run reproducibility record (environment.solidaritynode) and the documentation site footer.

Model versions (for example diagnostic-v0 0.2.1) and data package versions are separate and recorded on every run.

docs.title: What a release must include
docs.text:
• [ ] Every merged change since the last release has a line under Unreleased in CHANGELOG.md, and the affected user guide pages are updated.
  • [ ] UAT passed on the release commit: make uat, then the current checklists in docs/uat/, by the maintainer.
  • [ ] CI green on main: lint, tests, end-to-end, docs, licences.
  • [ ] Migrations: every new Alembic migration listed in the changelog, with what it does to existing data.
  • [ ] Upgrade notes for installations in the changelog section: new or changed settings (.env.example), migrations, data package or scenario schema changes, anything an administrator must do, and whether a backup is needed first.
  • [ ] Known limitations stated.

flowchart LR
    A["branch release/vX.Y.Z"] --> B["CHANGELOG: Unreleased → X.Y.Z (date)"]
    B --> C["VERSION → X.Y.Z<br/>make version-sync"]
    C --> D["make lint test docs-build<br/>PR, CI, UAT"]
    D --> E["merge to main"]
    E --> F["tag vX.Y.Z on main"]
    F --> G["GitHub Release<br/>notes = changelog section"]
    F --> H["docs workflow publishes<br/>docs version X.Y (latest)"]
  1. On a branch release/vX.Y.Z: in CHANGELOG.md, rename Unreleased to [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD, start a new empty Unreleased section above it, and update the comparison links at the bottom.
  2. Write X.Y.Z into VERSION and run make version-sync.
  3. Run make lint test docs-build, open a PR titled chore(release): vX.Y.Z, wait for CI and UAT, merge.
  4. Tag the merge commit and push the tag (signed tags are welcome): 
    git switch main && git pull
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "SolidarityNode X.Y.Z"
git push origin vX.Y.Z
  5. Create the GitHub Release from the tag, with the changelog section of X.Y.Z as the notes: 
    gh release create vX.Y.Z --title "SolidarityNode X.Y.Z" --notes-file <(python3 - <<'PY'
import re, pathlib
text = pathlib.Path("CHANGELOG.md").read_text()
print(re.search(r"## \[X\.Y\.Z\][^\n]*\n(.*?)(?=\n## \[)", text, re.S).group(1).strip())
PY
)
  6. The tag starts the docs workflow, which publishes the documentation as version X.Y with the alias latest (the default version of the site). dev keeps following main.
  7. Update CITATION.cff (version, date-released) in the next PR if it was not done in the release PR.

docs.title: Documentation versions
docs.text:
The site is versioned with mike: dev is built from main on every push, and each release tag vX.Y.Z publishes X.Y (patch releases overwrite their minor version) and moves latest to it. The version selector at the top of the site lists them.

One-time setup (maintainer): in the repository settings, Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source: Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root). The branch is created by the first run of the docs workflow on main. The site is then at https://solidaritynode.github.io/snode/.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
The order of work and what each step gives users. The live state (issues, who works on what, what is done) is on GitHub, never copied here: the Kintsugi board and the milestones.

flowchart LR
    F["1. Platform foundation<br/>v0.1"] --> H["2. Hub onboarding<br/>v0.2"]
    H --> P1["3. Paper 1, v0.3<br/>accessibility, capacity"]
    P1 --> P2["4. Paper 2, v0.4<br/>hidden need"]
    P2 --> P3["5. Paper 3, v0.5<br/>vulnerability"]
    P3 --> P4["6. Paper 4, v0.6<br/>operations, resilience"]

Each paper step starts only when its open questions are decided (open questions) and its per-paper spec is written (specifications). Each step is one minor version: v0.1 to v0.6 (the milestones carry the same names).

Step What it delivers for users Milestone Issues 1. Platform foundation (0.1.0) Sign-in and roles; the study area on a map with data quality and edge-effect warnings; versioned "what if" scenarios; background runs with progress, cancel and full reproducibility; results with uncertainty, comparison and export; data packages with preview, update and rollback. Results come from the diagnostic model only. v0.1 Platform foundation board 2. Hub onboarding (v0.2) The hub role: national sources, step-by-step onboarding of a municipality with a coverage matrix, facility imports from Excel, CSV or GeoPackage with an error report, publication of packages, and a notice to neighbours whose data improves. Real (open) data for a first study area. v0.2 Hub onboarding board 3. Paper 1: accessibility and capacity (v0.3) Travel times by group and mode; supply per area with shared facilities (2SFCA); the service gap by group with the reason (capacity, access or demand); the first research results, with uncertainty and sensitivity. v0.3 Paper 1 Accessibility label paper:1 4. Paper 2: hidden need (v0.4) The share of each group with need that is never expressed, with an interval; maps of where recorded demand underestimates need. v0.4 Paper 2 Hidden need label paper:2 5. Paper 3: vulnerability (v0.5) What each group loses when facilities degrade or roads close, given the alternatives; maps at standard reference scenarios; how many people are affected and how deeply. v0.5 Paper 3 Vulnerability label paper:3 6. Paper 4: operations and resilience (v0.6) Anonymous request logging (after the privacy rules, ADR 0010); operational indicators and facility states; monitoring of recovery and resilience by area, group and service; estimates that learn from real operation. v0.6 Paper 4 Resilience label paper:4

What each step means for the method: domain model and paper revisions. What changed in each release: changelog.
