docs.title: 0001. Monorepo with core, backend, frontend
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: AGENTS.md "Architecture rules"

docs.title: Context
docs.text: SolidarityNode has a modelling library, an API and a web UI that change together while the method is being designed. Contributors include researchers who mainly touch the specs and core. Specs, code and decisions must stay cross-referenced.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Monorepo (core/, backend/, frontend/, docs/, .github/): one PR can change spec, model and API together; one CI; one issue tracker.
  2. Separate repositories per component: clearer ownership and independent releases, but cross-cutting changes need coordinated PRs and the spec drifts from the code.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use a monorepo. core is a standalone Python package (solidaritynode-core) that the backend consumes through a local path dependency. Dependency direction is backend → core; core never imports backend, frontend, web frameworks or database drivers.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• CI workflows use paths filters so a change only runs the affected component.
  • The core independence rule is enforced by tests and a lint rule, so core can be split into its own repository later without changes.
  • Each component keeps its own lockfile (core/uv.lock, backend/uv.lock, frontend/pnpm-lock.yaml).

docs.title: 0002. AGPL-3.0 licence
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: LICENSE, TRADEMARK.md, AGENTS.md "Licensing"

docs.title: Context
docs.text: SolidarityNode is public-interest research software for social services. It is likely to be offered as a hosted service (for example by a municipality or a contractor). Improvements made in such deployments should remain available to the public.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. AGPL-3.0: copyleft that also covers network use; modified hosted versions must publish their source.
  2. GPL-3.0: copyleft, but hosting a modified version without distributing it does not trigger source release.
  3. Permissive (MIT/Apache-2.0): widest reuse, including closed derivatives.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: License the project under AGPL-3.0-or-later (the LICENSE file holds the AGPL-3.0 text; package metadata uses the SPDX identifier AGPL-3.0-or-later). The project name is not covered by the licence; see TRADEMARK.md.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• New dependencies must have AGPL-compatible licences (MIT, BSD, Apache-2.0, ISC, MPL-2.0, LGPL, GPL-3.0, AGPL-3.0). scripts/check_licenses.py and the licenses workflow enforce this; each PR states the licence of new dependencies.
  • Contributions are accepted under the same licence with a DCO sign-off (no CLA).
  • -or-later was confirmed by the maintainer (2026-11-24): later versions of the AGPL published by the FSF may also be used.

docs.title: 0003. Core data model and the indexed-values container
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: docs/specs/00-domain-model.md §2–4, OQ-1, OQ-6, OQ-24, OQ-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The unit of analysis is spatial unit × social group × service × time (Paper 4 §3). Many quantities omit some of these dimensions (for example SS_{i,g,s} has no time; DemandRate^g has only group and service) or add others (facility, mode, scenario, Monte Carlo sample, discrete state). Outputs must carry uncertainty (AGENTS.md invariant 6). Quantities of different services must never be summed (OQ-24), and groups may overlap (OQ-6).

We need (a) immutable typed entities and (b) one container for indexed values that every module can share.

docs.title: Options for the container
docs.text:
1. xarray DataArray (Apache-2.0): named dimensions and labelled coordinates, broadcasting by name, NumPy-backed, optional Dask/Zarr/NetCDF, interoperates with pandas. Adds xarray + pandas as dependencies.
  2. pandas DataFrame with a MultiIndex: familiar, good I/O, but sparse long format, no named broadcasting, and easy to mis-align.
  3. Typed wrapper over plain NumPy with our own dimension metadata: no extra dependency, but we would reimplement labelled selection, alignment and I/O.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Entities are frozen dataclasses with validation in __post_init__ (no Pydantic in core, to keep it light and framework-free).
  • Indexed values use IndexedValues, a thin immutable wrapper over xarray.DataArray (core/src/solidaritynode_core/model/indexed.py):
  • only dimensions from the Dim enum are allowed (unit, facility, group, service, mode, scenario, time, state, sample), named after the OQ-1 notation; any subset may be present, so absent dimensions are natural;
  • coordinate labels must be unique; values are copied and read-only;
  • check_aligned refuses mismatched shared dimensions;
  • sum_over(SERVICE) is refused (OQ-24) and sum_over(GROUP) is refused while overlap handling is open (OQ-6);
  • to_dataarray() gives a copy for library interop.
  • Uncertain scalars are PointValue | Samples | DiscreteDistribution; arrays carry uncertainty in a sample or state dimension.
  • ServiceQuantity carries service, service unit and reference period; adding quantities that differ in any of them raises UnitMismatchError (OQ-24, OQ-25).
  • Geometry is typed as any object with __geo_interface__, so core needs no geometry library yet (GeoPandas/Shapely arrive with the accessibility module).
  • Scenarios are overlays on the baseline (Spec 00 §3). Besides disruption severities, network disruption, rationing case and reference level, Scenario.interventions holds typed what-if placeholders (CapacityChange, absolute or relative; NewFacility; Paper 1 §13) with no behaviour. The JSON schema and versioning of stored scenarios are ADR 0016.
  • A variable catalogue (model/catalogue.py) mirrors Spec 00 §4 and records each variable's kind (BN node, computed, parameter, output…) and dimensions, so tests can keep these categories distinct.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• core depends on numpy and xarray (and transitively pandas, packaging); all BSD/Apache licensed.
  • The wrapper hides most of xarray's API on purpose; modules that need more can use to_dataarray() internally and wrap the result again.
  • Storage of large arrays (Parquet vs Zarr/NetCDF) is a separate decision (ADR 0008).
  • If performance or typing becomes an issue, the wrapper keeps the public API stable while the backend changes.

docs.title: Demo data in the database (temporary)
docs.text: The synthetic demo dataset (data/synthetic/demo/, DP-001) is loaded by make seed into a separate PostgreSQL schema demo (Alembic migration 0002), never into public. Its tables mirror the demo files, not this data model, and exist only so tests and UAT can inspect realistic-looking data. The demo schema is temporary and will be replaced by data-package import in the platform PR (ADR 0013). The loader copies data and computes nothing.

docs.title: 0004. BN/DBN library
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed (stub, needs a human decision)
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: OQ-7, OQ-17, OQ-27; AGENTS.md stack (pgmpy, "evaluate limits via ADR before committing")

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Papers 1–3 need discrete Bayesian networks with expert-elicited CPTs and posterior queries; Paper 2 and Paper 4 need parameter learning of CPTs with an expert CPT as prior (OQ-8, OQ-16, OQ-27); Paper 4 needs a dynamic BN (OQ-17). Inference runs inside Monte Carlo loops, so speed matters. core.bayes defines the interfaces; this ADR picks the engine behind them.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. pgmpy (MIT): Python, discrete BNs, variable elimination and belief propagation, Bayesian parameter estimation with Dirichlet priors, DynamicBayesianNetwork class. Check: DBN support is limited to two-slice models and its inference options; performance inside Monte Carlo; maturity of soft evidence.
  2. pomegranate (MIT): fast, PyTorch-based; check current BN support and API stability.
  3. PyAgrum (LGPL-3.0 or MIT, verify): mature C++ core, BNs, DBNs (2TBN), learning; check licence terms and packaging.
  4. Own implementation of the small fixed networks (exact enumeration over few nodes) behind core.bayes, possibly with NumPy vectorisation across units.
  5. Probabilistic programming (PyMC, NumPyro) for parameter learning only, combined with one of the above for discrete inference.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Can the engine evaluate the same network for thousands of (unit, group, service, sample) cells efficiently, or do we need vectorised custom code?
  • Does it support Dirichlet priors with configurable equivalent sample size per row (OQ-27) and learning from incomplete data?
  • What DBN structures does it support (OQ-17), and how would we unroll over time?
  • Licence compatibility with AGPL-3.0 and long-term maintenance.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Not decided.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: To be written with the decision.

docs.title: 0005. Inference approach, CPT size and discretisation
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed (stub, needs a human decision)
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: OQ-7, OQ-11, OQ-15, OQ-4

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Continuous quantities (service gap ratio, Group Exposure, Service Loss, need-based gap, access deterrence) enter discrete BNs. Thresholds for Group Exposure and Service Loss are open (OQ-15); the relation between the deterministic Service Gap and its BN node is open (OQ-4). The non-take-up node has four three-state parents, giving 81 CPT rows (OQ-11), which is hard to elicit.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. Fixed thresholds per variable, documented in configuration (simple; sensitive to the cut points).
  2. Soft/virtual evidence from the continuous value (likelihoods over states) instead of hard discretisation.
  3. Quantile-based thresholds from the baseline distribution (data-driven; not comparable across areas).
  4. For large CPTs: intermediate nodes (for example combining access deterrence and outside alternatives), ranked nodes or other parametric elicitation (Fenton et al.; verify reference), or noisy-OR/MAX style models.
  5. Exact inference (enumeration / variable elimination) vs sampling; with networks this small, exact is likely feasible.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Which variables are discretised, with which states and thresholds, and who sets them (experts, data)?
  • Hard vs soft evidence, and how this interacts with Monte Carlo (sample, then discretise?).
  • How are implausible parent combinations flagged or skipped during elicitation (OQ-11)?
  • Elicitation protocol: frequency format, number of experts, aggregation.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Not decided.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: To be written with the decision.

docs.title: 0006. Background job queue
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-24 (accepted for v0.1: 2026-11-25)
  • Related: AGENTS.md "Long-running simulations run as background jobs"; backend/src/solidaritynode_backend/jobs/

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Monte Carlo runs and scenario sweeps can take minutes to hours and must not run inside a request handler. The bootstrap provides a JobRunner protocol and an in-process thread-pool runner for development only (jobs are lost on restart, no result storage, no retries).

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. PostgreSQL-backed queue (for example procrastinate, or SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED by hand): no new infrastructure; check licences (procrastinate is MIT).
  2. RQ (BSD) or Dramatiq (LGPL-3.0) with Redis/Valkey: simple workers; adds a service.
  3. Celery (BSD): feature-rich, heavier.
  4. Arq (MIT): asyncio, Redis.
  5. Keep jobs as separate containers/processes started per run.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Expected run duration, concurrency and need for cancellation/progress reporting?
  • Should job state live in PostGIS with the run metadata?
  • How do workers access Parquet outputs (shared volume, object storage)?
  • Rootless Podman compatibility of the extra services.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited: option 1, a PostgreSQL-backed queue written by hand (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), consumed by a separate worker process.

  • Jobs are rows in table jobs (kind, JSON payload, status queued → running → succeeded | failed | cancelled, progress 0–100, error, cancel_requested, worker name, timestamps, heartbeat_at).
  • Claiming commits before execution. The worker claims the oldest queued job with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and sets it running in one short transaction, which commits before the handler starts. No transaction or row lock is held while a job runs, so the API can read and flag the job and a sweep can fail it (backend/tests/test_worker.py::test_claim_commits_before_the_job_runs).
  • The bootstrap JobRunner interface is kept but evolved: a job is a kind plus a JSON payload (not a Python callable, so it can cross processes), and the interface gains cancel. The in-process thread-pool runner is removed. PostgresJobRunner implements it; routers depend only on the interface.
  • The worker (python -m solidaritynode_backend.worker) is its own compose service with the backend image. It runs one job at a time, reports progress to the job row, stops a job at its next progress step when cancellation is requested, and marks the running job failed with a clear message on SIGTERM/SIGINT.
  • Lease and heartbeat. While a job runs, a separate thread of its worker sets jobs.heartbeat_at = now() every SOLIDARITYNODE_JOB_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS (default 10). Any worker, at start and then every heartbeat interval while idle, marks running jobs whose heartbeat is older than SOLIDARITYNODE_JOB_STALE_SECONDS (default 120, at least twice the heartbeat) as failed ("Interrupted: the worker (…) stopped while this run was running (no heartbeat since …). No results were stored. Start the run again."). A worker never overwrites a job that is no longer running, so a swept job stays failed. The worker name (SOLIDARITYNODE_WORKER_NAME) is recorded for logs only; recovery no longer depends on it.
  • Maximum runtime per job kind (optional, SOLIDARITYNODE_JOB_MAX_RUNTIME_SECONDS, for example run=3600; default empty, so the diagnostic model's run jobs have no limit). A job over its limit is stopped at its next progress step, like a cancel, and marked failed ("Stopped: the job ran longer than the maximum runtime of … s set for '…' jobs …").
  • Outputs are shared through the results volume mounted in both containers (ADR 0008).

Maintainer decision (2026-11-25, PR #6): the evolved interface (submit(kind, payload) plus cancel) and the removal of the in-process runner are accepted.

Why: no new service or dependency, job state lives next to the run metadata in one transaction, rootless Podman needs nothing extra, and runs are short at this stage. Cancellation and progress are simple column updates.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Polling (1 s) adds a little latency; LISTEN/NOTIFY can replace it later.
  • One worker process, one job at a time. Several workers are possible (SKIP LOCKED, and the lease does not depend on names).
  • A killed worker's job is failed only after SOLIDARITYNODE_JOB_STALE_SECONDS (default 2 minutes), not at the instant of restart; a busy worker sweeps only after its current job.
  • Cancellation and the maximum runtime are cooperative: they act at the handler's next progress step. A handler that never reports progress cannot be stopped this way (the diagnostic model reports at every step).
  • No retries or scheduling.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text:
Replace the hand-written queue when any of these happens:

  1. a run takes longer than 10 minutes;
  2. more than one user regularly waits for runs at the same time;
  3. scheduled jobs are needed (for example periodic imports or reports);
  4. retries for external calls are needed (for example downloads from the hub or open data services).

First candidate: procrastinate (MIT, PostgreSQL only: no new service, keeps job state next to the run metadata). RQ, Dramatiq or Celery remain options if a broker becomes acceptable. The JobRunner interface keeps the change local to jobs/ and the worker. The hub-onboarding PR (ADR 0012, 0014) is likely to hit triggers 3 and 4 (scheduled package builds and calls to external sources), so revisit this ADR there.

docs.title: 0007. Frontend map library
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-24 (accepted for v0.1: 2026-11-25)
  • Related: README "Planned capabilities"; frontend/

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The frontend will show indicators per spatial unit, group and service, with uncertainty (AGENTS.md invariant 6), and vulnerability maps at reference scenarios (OQ-16). No map library is installed yet.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. MapLibre GL JS (BSD-3-Clause): vector tiles, WebGL, styling; good for many polygons.
  2. Leaflet (BSD-2-Clause): simple, raster-first, large plugin ecosystem.
  3. OpenLayers (BSD-2-Clause): full GIS feature set, heavier API.
  4. deck.gl (MIT) on top of MapLibre for large data layers.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Basemap source and its licence/attribution (OpenStreetMap tiles usage policy; self-hosted tiles?).
  • How uncertainty is shown (intervals, small multiples, hatching).
  • Accessibility (keyboard, screen readers, colour-blind palettes).
  • Bundle size and React integration.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited: option 2, Leaflet (BSD-2-Clause), used directly with a small React wrapper (frontend/src/map/MapView.tsx). react-leaflet is not used: its licence (Hippocratic-2.1) is not compatible with AGPL-3.0.

  • Basemap configurable with SOLIDARITYNODE_BASEMAP: osm (OpenStreetMap standard tiles with the required attribution, light interactive use within the OSMF tile usage policy) or blank (no tiles, for offline use and tests).
  • The backend reprojects layers to EPSG:4326 with PostGIS; the frontend only displays.
  • Styling: core units solid, buffer units grey and dashed; quality shown with SVG patterns (hatching = estimated, dots = open data); edge-effect units with an orange outline; results in viridis (sequential) and PuOr (diverging), both readable with common colour-vision deficiencies.
  • Uncertainty on maps (AGENTS.md invariant 6). Results maps and per-unit tables show the median and its interval (ADR 0017); the mean is stored and exported, not mapped. Every displayed value names its statistic: column headings "Median (90 % interval)", tooltips "Unit A3, median (90 % interval): 0.42 (0.31–0.55)", legend titles "…, median (min)" and the note under each map. The interval name comes from the run's quantile levels ("90 % interval" for 0.05/0.95, "10–95 % quantile interval" for asymmetric levels, "interval (levels not recorded)" for older runs); comparison headings name each run's interval. Differences are "Difference of medians A − B". An Uncertainty toggle (off by default) adds a second map of the interval width (high − low) in its own palette (Blues), next to the value map; on comparison screens it switches maps A and B to the width. Hatching and dots are never used for uncertainty: they mean data quality. Tooltips and tables always show the interval with the median, for example 0.42 (0.31–0.55); deterministic values say so. Probability outputs (indicator unit probability) use a fixed 0–1 scale (classes of 0.2) labelled as a probability, never a range stretched to the data.
  • Comparison screens (baseline vs scenario, and the same scenario across data versions) build one colour scale from the values of both runs and show one legend for maps A and B, so equal values have equal colours (test: frontend/src/pages/ComparePage.test.tsx). The difference map keeps its own diverging scale and legend.
  • Data-quality layer. On results and comparison maps the quality patterns are a toggleable layer, off by default, so they do not hide the value colours; the results table always marks units of estimated or open_data quality in words, and a note says how many there are. The study-area screen always shows the patterns.
  • Referrer. Map tiles must be requested with a valid Referer (OSMF tile usage policy). nginx sends Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin on every response and the Leaflet tile layer sets the same policy on its tile images; never use no-referrer or same-origin (checked by the end-to-end test).
  • Accessibility: the map container is keyboard-focusable (arrows pan, +/- zoom), every map has a text list of its features and a legend in words.

Why: the demo and first municipalities have few polygons, so raster-first Leaflet is enough; it is small, well known and simple to wrap without a React binding.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Layer size triggers: above about 1,000 features in one map, switch Leaflet to its canvas renderer (preferCanvas) instead of SVG. Above about 2,000 polygons, or for national views in the hub, revisit with MapLibre GL JS (BSD-3-Clause) and vector tiles. Note that the canvas renderer cannot use the SVG quality patterns as they are; that change needs its own quality marking.
  • OpenStreetMap's public tile servers are for development and demos only. The OSMF Tile Usage Policy (https://operations.osmfoundation.org/policies/tiles/) gives no SLA and allows access to be withdrawn at any time without notice. Production installations need their own tiles or a tile provider whose terms cover their traffic.
  • Basemap options for later (none implemented now; the osm | blank setting stays for v0.1):
  • Preferred for production: self-hosted PMTiles (Protomaps). The hub produces one basemap extract per data package (same extent as the study area), served as a static file by the installation itself: no tile server, no third-party traffic, works offline.
  • For demos and pilots: OpenFreeMap, a free hosted vector-tile service, when self-hosting is not yet set up.
  • Both are vector basemaps. When vector basemaps are adopted, MapLibre GL JS (BSD-3-Clause) is the candidate replacement for Leaflet; record that change in a new ADR.
  • Leaflet stays for v0.1.

docs.title: 0008. Storage of large arrays (Parquet)
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-24 (accepted for v0.1: 2026-11-25)
  • Related: AGENTS.md "Large datasets live in files (Parquet)"; ADR 0003

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Results are indexed by unit × group × service × time plus scenario and Monte Carlo sample, and can be large. AGENTS.md states that large datasets live in Parquet files with metadata and result indexes in PostgreSQL/PostGIS. core represents arrays as IndexedValues (xarray, ADR 0003).

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. Parquet in long format (one row per cell and sample) via PyArrow (Apache-2.0) or Polars (MIT); GeoParquet for geometries.
  2. Zarr or NetCDF for dense labelled arrays (native for xarray).
  3. Both: Parquet for tabular inputs, Zarr for dense result cubes.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Where do files live (local volume, S3-compatible object storage) and how are they referenced from the database index?
  • Partitioning (by run, scenario, service) and retention.
  • Does storing per-sample results raise privacy concerns when units are small (OQ-21)?
  • Should core own the I/O, or the backend (keeping core free of storage concerns)?

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited: option 1, Parquet in long format via PyArrow (Apache-2.0), written by the backend (core stays free of I/O).

  • Per-sample values: <results_dir>/runs/<run_id>/samples.parquet, columns unit_id, group_id, service_id, time_label, indicator, sample, value; results_dir is the results volume (/data/results in compose). The run row stores the path.
  • Sample semantics. sample identifies one joint Monte Carlo draw shared by all cells of a run: draw i uses the same values of every shared uncertain parameter across units, groups and services. Models must sample jointly, never independently per cell, so totals computed sample by sample (ADR 0017, summarise_total) have correct intervals. This is part of the model registry contract (CellSamples, ModelResult, which also requires every cell to have the same number of draws). diagnostic-v0 complies since version 0.2.0: draw i has one shared factor plus an independent term per cell (each cell standard normal, correlation 0.5 between cells); 0.1.0 drew every cell independently. Core test test_samples_are_joint_draws_so_totals_across_units_use_the_same_index.
  • Layout (results schema version 1): id columns dictionary-encoded; value stored as float32 unless the model declares float64 (ModelSpec.sample_dtype), and the summary statistics are computed from the values at that precision, so they can be reproduced exactly from the file; sample as int32; rows sorted by indicator, unit, group, service, time and sample; zstd compression.
  • Metadata and integrity. The Parquet key-value metadata (solidaritynode.*) records the run id, model id and version, data package id and version, data version id, results schema version, value precision and sort order. The file's SHA-256 is stored on the run row (runs.samples_sha256, shown under Reproducibility and in metadata.json) and verified on every read (services.samples.read_samples) and export: a missing, changed or foreign file is refused (export answers 409). Runs stored before migration 0006 have no checksum and are not checked.
  • Size estimate. Before a run starts, its samples file size is estimated from the run configuration and the data version: draws × core units × groups × services × sampled indicators × 28 bytes (float32; an upper bound before compression). Above SOLIDARITYNODE_SAMPLES_WARN_MB (default 500) the backend logs a warning and the run page shows one; the run is still queued. The estimate and the limit are stored on the run.
  • Summary values per unit × group × service × time (mean, median and interval quantiles, ADR 0017) in table run_results; model tables (travel_times, unit_changes) as JSON in run_tables.
  • Files are written to a temporary name and renamed, so a crash never leaves a partial file referenced by a run.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No retention or partitioning yet; one file per run. Revisit with object storage or Zarr when Monte Carlo sample counts grow.
  • Back up results together with the database. The run row points to its samples file and records its checksum; a database backup without the results volume (or the reverse) leaves runs whose samples cannot be read or verified. Back up both at the same point in time and restore them together.
  • OQ-21 (clarification, the question stays open). Model samples are estimates produced by a model from aggregate inputs, not records of people. The privacy limits of OQ-21 (minimum cell sizes, aggregation, retention) apply mainly to quantities derived from tickets (Paper 4: observed requests, take-up, consequences), and to any model output that reproduces them at a fine level. Revisit when ticket-derived quantities enter a model.

docs.title: 0009. Geospatial data sources
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed (stub, needs a human decision)
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: OQ-22, docs/data-sources.md, Spec 00 §3 (networks, DEM)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Accessibility (Paper 1 §5) needs spatial units, population by group, facilities, per-mode transport networks (road, pedestrian, public transport) and a DEM. The first application uses Greek Local Communities (ΤΚ), but code must stay generic (OQ-22). Every third-party source must be attributed and its licence respected.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via OSMnx (MIT) for road and pedestrian networks; attribution and share-alike obligations for derived databases.
  2. GTFS feeds for public transport, where published (licence per operator).
  3. ELSTAT census data and administrative boundaries for population by group (terms to check).
  4. Copernicus DEM or EU-DEM for elevation (licence to check).
  5. Facility registries from public bodies (licence to check).

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Which sources exist for the first study area, at what resolution and with which licences?
  • How are ODbL share-alike obligations handled for derived travel-time matrices?
  • Update frequency and versioning of inputs.
  • Which synthetic equivalents do we ship in data/synthetic/ for tests?

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Not decided.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: To be written with the decision.

docs.title: 0010. Privacy rules for request tickets
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed (stub, needs a human decision)
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: OQ-21, OQ-29, OQ-6, OQ-8; AGENTS.md "Data and privacy rules"; core.model.Ticket

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Tickets are anonymous by design (spatial unit, group, service, the facility where the request is made or scheduled, timestamps, a yes/no "first request in this period" flag). The facility was added by OQ-29 (decided 2026-11-24): facility state, facility output and recording coverage (Paper 4 §5, §14; OQ-8) need it. In small units, the combination of unit, group, facility and timestamps can still identify people (OQ-21); the facility makes cells smaller, so every rule below applies to it too (OQ-29). These rules also limit how finely observations can be used for learning (OQ-8, OQ-16). No ticket may be stored before this ADR is accepted.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. Minimum cell size (k-anonymity) for any stored or published aggregate; suppression or merging of small cells.
  2. Timestamp coarsening (for example to the day or week) at capture time, with exact durations kept only as derived waiting times.
  3. Retention limits: raw tickets deleted after aggregation into period counts.
  4. Aggregation before storage: store only counts per (unit, group, service, period).
  5. Differential privacy for published aggregates.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• What is the minimum cell size, and does it apply to storage, publication or both?
  • Which waiting-time indicators (Paper 4 §4.2) survive timestamp coarsening?
  • How is the "first request in this period" flag set without storing an identifier (OQ-8)?
  • How are people in several groups recorded (OQ-6)?
  • Does the minimum cell size apply to unit × group × service × facility × period, or are facilities aggregated first (OQ-29)?
  • GDPR assessment (DPIA) for deployments.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Not decided.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: To be written with the decision.

docs.title: 0011. Container engine (Podman default, Docker supported)
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed (stub, needs a human decision)
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: AGENTS.md "Stack"; Makefile, compose.yaml

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Contributors work on Linux, macOS and Windows/WSL2. AGENTS.md sets Podman (rootless) as the default engine and requires Docker to keep working. The bootstrap implements this: the Makefile defines CONTAINER_ENGINE ?= podman and COMPOSE ?= podman compose; images use fully qualified names; ports are non-privileged; no bind mounts; healthchecks live in compose.yaml because Podman's OCI image format ignores HEALTHCHECK; CI builds images with both engines.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. Podman default, Docker supported (current implementation).
  2. Docker default, Podman supported.
  3. Podman only.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Confirm the current implementation as the accepted decision.
  • Which compose provider is supported for Podman (podman compose delegating to podman-compose or docker-compose)? Verified locally with podman-compose 1.5.0.
  • Should CI also run the full stack (make up) with both engines, not only image builds?

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Not decided.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: To be written with the decision.

docs.title: 0012. Deployment model: municipal installations and a hub
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-24 (accepted for v0.1: 2026-11-25)
  • Related: Spec 00 §3 (Deployment, Onboarding, Data package), OQ-21, OQ-28; ADR 0013, 0014, 0015

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Spec 00 §3 describes one codebase running in two roles: a municipal installation (it serves one study area of one or more core municipalities, with its own users, scenarios, runs and tickets) and a hub (national raw sources, onboarding, curated data, data packages, optional aggregated indicators shared upwards). Tickets and operational data must stay inside the municipality (AGENTS.md privacy rules, OQ-21). Everything must keep running locally with make up (Podman default, Docker supported).

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. One codebase, role chosen by configuration (for example APP_ROLE=municipality | hub): routers, jobs and UI sections enabled per role; one image.
  2. Separate hub service in the same monorepo sharing core, with its own backend and database.
  3. Single multi-tenant installation hosting several municipalities. Simpler to operate, but weakens the "tickets never leave the municipality" property and the privacy boundary of OQ-21.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Which features exist only in the hub (raw sources, onboarding, package publishing) and which only in installations (tickets, local runs)?
  • How does an installation obtain packages (pull from the hub, manual import of a file)? Must it work offline?
  • Who operates installations (municipal IT, a regional body, the project)? What are the minimum hardware requirements?
  • How is the role reflected in /version and the UI so testers know which role they are using?

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited: option 1, one codebase, role chosen by configuration, with the setting DEPLOYMENT_MODE=municipality | hub (default municipality).

  • An installation serves one study area of one or more core municipalities (plus its buffer, OQ-28). In this version only the municipal installation works fully: its own users, scenarios and runs, data obtained by manual import of package files (works offline).
  • hub starts the same services but offers no hub features yet (onboarding is the next PR).
  • GET /config exposes the mode so the UI and testers can see it.
  • Role lock. The role is stored in the database (table installation, one row) when it is first initialised (migration 0007, from DEPLOYMENT_MODE). The API, the worker and the CLI refuse to start when DEPLOYMENT_MODE differs from it, with a message naming both roles. One database serves one role; switching role means a new database (backend/tests/test_roles.py).
  • Role separation. Routers of the other role are not mounted (not merely disabled): their paths answer 404 and are absent from the OpenAPI schema. Ticket routes (/requests) exist only in municipality, hub routes (/hub) only in hub; each has one read-only status endpoint for now. Tables of one role are created only by migrations guarded by the stored role (services.installation.stored_role), so ticket tables never exist in the hub; none exist yet (ADR 0010). The exported docs/schemas/openapi.json describes the municipal installation.

Why: the simplest option that keeps both roles in one image and leaves the hub open.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• UI sections will be enabled per role when hub features exist.
  • Pulling packages from the hub, upward flow (ADR 0014) and multi-tenancy are not implemented.
  • Commitment for any future connection (not implemented now). Every connection between an installation and the hub is initiated by the installation (outbound only): it pulls packages and, if ADR 0014 allows, pushes what it chose to share. The hub never connects into an installation, needs no inbound access to it and holds no credentials for it. The municipality controls what is sent and when; nothing leaves an installation without that decision.

docs.title: Open questions (kept open)
docs.text:
• Operator: who runs installations (municipal IT, a regional body, the project) and the hub.
  • Minimum hardware for an installation and for the hub.
  • Update policy: who updates installations, how often, and how database migrations and data packages are rolled out.
  • Public exposure: how an installation is reached from outside its machine (reverse proxy with HTTPS, certificates, which ports). Today everything binds to 127.0.0.1.

These belong to a future "production operations" ADR (together with backups of the database and the results volume, ADR 0008).

docs.title: 0013. Data packages: format, versioning, checksums and buffer
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-24 (accepted for v0.1: 2026-11-25)
  • Related: Spec 00 §3 (Data package, Study area, Onboarding, Stable identifiers), OQ-28; ADR 0003, 0008, 0009, 0012; docs/data-processing/README.md rule 9

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Spec 00 §3: a data package is a versioned (semantic versioning), checksummed bundle for one study area plus a buffer of neighbouring units (OQ-28), with layer coverage, changelog and provenance, produced by the hub and imported by an installation after a preview of changes. Features keep stable ids and carry municipality_id, role (core | buffer), quality, valid_from / valid_to. Each package's manifest.json lists the DP-NNN processing notes behind its data (docs/data-processing/README.md, rule 9).

docs.title: History
docs.text: The bootstrap used a draft manifest (format_version: "0.1-draft", still in data/synthetic/demo/manifest.json, the source dataset of DP-001) and a temporary demo schema loaded by make seed. Both are replaced by the format and import below (migration 0003 drops the demo schema; the demo packages are built by DP-002).

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. Directory or zip of GeoPackage + CSV/Parquet + manifest.json (as in the demo): opens in QGIS, simple to check.
  2. Single GeoPackage containing all layers, tables and the manifest as a table.
  3. Frictionless Data Package (datapackage.json) conventions, extended with spatial metadata.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Exact layer list and schemas (with ADR 0003 and ADR 0009); large arrays in Parquet (ADR 0008).
  • Buffer definition (OQ-28) and how buffer features are marked and reported.
  • Import workflow: preview of changes (added, changed, closed features), validation, rollback.
  • Signing in addition to checksums? Where are packages published?
  • How do runs record the package version for reproducibility (ADR 0017)?

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited: option 1, a directory or archive (.zip, .tar, .tar.gz) with a manifest.json, one GeoPackage with the layers and CSV tables. Schema version 2.0.

Why schema 2.0 (GeoPackage instead of GeoJSON). Schema 1.0 stored the layers as GeoJSON with coordinates in EPSG:2100 and the obsolete GeoJSON 2008 crs member. RFC 7946 GeoJSON allows only WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) longitude/latitude, so those files were not valid GeoJSON and other tools could misread them. Schema 2.0 keeps the projected CRS declared in the manifest (distances and areas in metres, as the network and accessibility need) in a format that declares it properly: one GeoPackage layers.gpkg with one table per layer. It is read and written with the standard library (backend/src/solidaritynode_backend/gpkg.py, the bootstrap's writer plus a reader), opens in QGIS, and is built byte-for-byte reproducibly. Schema 1.x packages are refused with the usual "schema version not supported" message.

manifest.json keys: format (solidaritynode-data-package), schema_version (MAJOR.MINOR; an installation reads one major version and refuses others with a clear message), package_id, version (semantic versioning), created, synthetic, description, crs (EPSG:n), study_area (core_municipalities, buffer_municipalities), buffer (rule, description; the definition is open, OQ-28), coverage (per municipality and layer boundaries, population, network, facilities, transit: status missing | open_data | estimated | verified_by_municipality and the layer version), layers (per layer: table in layers.gpkg, geometry_type, licence, attribution; all required), sources (name, licence, attribution), processing_notes (DP-NNN, required), changelog (must contain the package version), files (path, sha256, bytes for every file; unlisted files are refused).

Files: layers.gpkg with tables municipalities, spatial_units, facilities, network_nodes, network_edges (geometry column geom, 2D, every table in the manifest CRS: a layer in another CRS is refused with a message naming both), tables/{groups,services, population,facility_services}.csv, checks/hand_check_travel_times.csv (optional). The reader opens the GeoPackage read-only with trusted_schema off, runs quick_check, and refuses non-GeoPackage files, Z/M coordinates and extended geometry blobs.

CSV dialect: UTF-8 (a leading byte-order mark is tolerated), comma delimiter, dot as decimal separator, one header row with the expected column names, numeric columns as plain numbers. Anything else is refused with a message that says what to change, for example a semicolon delimiter or comma decimals from a Greek-locale spreadsheet, or a Windows-1253 file.

One name for the verified state: verified_by_municipality, for feature quality and layer coverage alike (coverage used verified in schema 1.0; migration 0008 renamed stored rows). Every feature has a stable id (the same in every package and installation; for units the official statistical code where one exists, otherwise a hub-assigned id) and municipality_id, role (core | buffer), quality (open_data | estimated | verified_by_municipality), valid_from, valid_to and processing_note. Features are closed with valid_to, never deleted; a feature is open when valid_to is empty or after the package date.

Import (make import-package PKG=… or the Admin screen): validate the manifest, schema version and checksums → preview against the active version (added, changed, closed features per layer, coverage changes) → import after confirmation, in one transaction. Rules: the same version with the same manifest is a no-op; the same version with different content, a vanished feature or an incompatible schema is refused. Every imported version is kept (data_versions, data_features, data_records, data_coverage); the new one becomes active; runs keep their version. Each import creates a baseline run (empty scenario) on the new version. Scenarios are revalidated against it; references to closed or missing features are reported.

Rollback: an administrator can make an earlier imported version active again (Admin screen, make activate-version VERSION=x.y.z, POST /data-versions/{id}/activate). Like an import, it queues a baseline run on that version and revalidates every scenario; nothing is deleted.

Licences: every layer carries a licence and an attribution in the manifest (for example ODbL 1.0 with "© OpenStreetMap contributors" for OpenStreetMap-derived network layers). The Study area screen lists them. Distributing a package carries the obligations of each layer's licence (attribution, share-alike for ODbL derivatives, terms of official sources); legal review is needed before any package with real data is distributed.

Edge effects (OQ-28, warning only): a core unit whose geometry touches a buffer municipality with facilities: missing carries an edge-effect warning on maps and results.

The temporary demo schema is dropped by migration 0003.

Why: opens in QGIS, keeps the projected CRS properly declared, simple to check by hand, needs no new library to read or write.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every version is stored in full: fine for a municipality, revisit for large study areas.
  • Checksums detect corruption, not tampering: whoever can change a file can also change the manifest. Packages must be signed (and signatures verified) before any automatic download from the hub is added (ADR 0014); until then packages are imported by hand from a trusted source.
  • Large arrays in packages (Parquet) are not needed yet.

docs.title: Open for later (from UAT, no code now)
docs.text:
• How real data corrections reach the hub. Analysts never upload data: hypothetical changes are scenarios (docs/concepts.md), and real corrections or new facilities go to the hub and arrive in the next package version. How an analyst or a municipality submits such a correction (form, file, ticket, with which evidence and quality level) is part of the hub onboarding work (ADR 0012, 0014), not decided here.
  • Choice of spatial unit for large municipalities. For a municipality such as Athens, the 7 municipal communities are too coarse to show differences in access within it. Which spatial unit to use (census tracts, building blocks, a grid) is a method choice for the Paper 1 spec (Spec 01), not a package format question; the package format already carries whatever unit the spec chooses.

docs.title: 0014. Upward data flow from municipalities to the hub
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed (stub, needs a human decision)
  • Date: 2026-11-24
  • Related: Spec 00 §3 (Deployment), OQ-21, OQ-8, OQ-16, OQ-27; ADR 0010, 0012

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Spec 00 §3 allows municipal installations to share optional aggregated indicators upwards to the hub. Tickets are anonymous but can still identify people in small units when combined (OQ-21). Pooled learning across units (OQ-8 take-up, OQ-16 vulnerability relationship, OQ-27 priors) would benefit from data from several municipalities, but only if privacy holds.

docs.title: Constraints already stated
docs.text:
• Only aggregated, anonymised indicators leave an installation; never tickets or per-request records.
  • Opt-in per municipality, revocable, and visible to the municipality before anything is sent.
  • Aggregation and minimum cell sizes follow the rules decided for OQ-21 (ADR 0010); nothing flows until OQ-21 is decided.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. No upward flow in the first versions.
  2. Manual export of an aggregate file that the municipality reviews and sends.
  3. Automated push of aggregates on a schedule, after the municipality opts in.
  4. Privacy-enhancing techniques (for example differential-privacy noise on counts) on top of 2 or 3.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Which indicators are useful to the hub (and to which paper), at which spatial and temporal aggregation?
  • Minimum cell size and suppression rules (OQ-21), and how they interact with pooled learning (OQ-8, OQ-27).
  • Legal basis and data-protection impact assessment (GDPR); who is controller and processor.
  • Audit trail of what was sent and when.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Not decided.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: To be written. Nothing is sent upwards until this ADR and ADR 0010 are accepted.

docs.title: 0015. Authentication and roles
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-24 (accepted for v0.1: 2026-11-25)
  • Related: Spec 00 §3 (Scenario owner and visibility, Deployment), OQ-21; ADR 0010, 0012

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Scenarios have an owner and visibility (private, shared) (Spec 00 §3). Installations have their own users; the hub has its own. Tickets are entered by staff at facilities and must stay anonymous (AGENTS.md). The bootstrap has no authentication: all endpoints are open and the stack binds to 127.0.0.1 only.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. Built-in accounts in the backend (password hashing, sessions or tokens).
  2. External identity provider via OpenID Connect (for example Keycloak, Apache-2.0, run as an extra container), so municipalities can connect their own directory.
  3. Reverse-proxy authentication in front of the app, with roles passed in headers.

docs.title: Candidate roles (to confirm)
docs.text: Analyst or researcher (scenarios, runs, results), facility staff (ticket entry only), municipal administrator (users, data package import, upward sharing opt-in, ADR 0014), hub operator (onboarding, package publishing), read-only viewer.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Which roles are needed in each deployment role (ADR 0012)?
  • Must ticket entry work on shared devices without personal accounts (QR flow, Paper 4 §4.1), and how does that interact with OQ-21?
  • Audit logging requirements; session lifetime; password and MFA policy.
  • Licence of any identity component (must be AGPL-compatible).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited: option 1, built-in local accounts behind an IdentityProvider interface (backend/src/solidaritynode_backend/auth.py), so OpenID Connect can replace it later without changing routers.

  • Passwords hashed with Argon2id (argon2-cffi, MIT). Policy: at least 12 characters and not on a bundled list of common passwords (1,210 entries of 12+ characters from SecLists' NCSC list, MIT, backend/src/solidaritynode_backend/resources/common_passwords.txt; case is ignored); no composition rules (no forced digits or symbols). Applied wherever a password is set: user creation and change (API and Admin screen) and make create-admin. Existing hashes keep working.
  • Sign-in throttling per username and per client address (services/throttle.py, table login_throttle, migration 0009): after failure n the next attempt for that username is refused for 1 s × 2^(n-1) (at most 30 s); a client address is delayed the same way only from half its limit on (10 failures), so one person's typo does not delay colleagues behind the same office address; after 5 failures for a username or 20 for an address within 15 minutes it is locked for 15 minutes (all configurable, SOLIDARITYNODE_LOGIN_*). While delayed or locked the password is not checked and the answer is a generic 429 with Retry-After; wrong passwords and unknown users get the same 401 "wrong username or password", so neither reveals which accounts exist. Usernames and addresses are stored only as SHA-256 hashes. A successful sign-in clears both. A refused (429) attempt is not counted and never extends a delay or lock, so a lock ends at the stated time.
  • Client address (services/throttle.py, client_address): the TCP peer, unless the peer is a trusted proxy listed in SOLIDARITYNODE_TRUSTED_PROXIES (addresses or CIDR networks; default loopback and the private networks of the compose network). From a trusted proxy the backend takes X-Real-IP, or the nearest X-Forwarded-For entry that is not itself a proxy; headers from any other peer are ignored, so a client cannot choose its address. The bundled nginx overwrites both headers with the address it sees (uvicorn runs with --no-proxy-headers, so this is the only place headers are read). In production list only the reverse proxy and never publish the API port.
  • When the proxy cannot see the client. Behind rootless Podman's port forwarder every browser reaches nginx from nginx's own address (found in UAT: all sign-ins came from 10.89.0.6, so the per-address limit counted every user together and one person's mistakes locked out everyone). When the address a proxy reports is itself a trusted proxy address, the client address is unknown: only the per-username limit applies, and the backend logs a warning once. Failed tries for one username therefore never block another username there. Where client addresses are visible (Docker, rootful Podman, a production reverse proxy), the per-address limit applies as described above; on a shared office address it can still delay colleagues once that address reaches half its limit (10 failures).
  • Clearing locks. An administrator clears sign-in delays and locks with make clear-login-locks USERNAME=<name> (one username) or make clear-login-locks (all usernames and addresses); see docs/uat/README.md.
  • Opaque session token in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie (Secure with SOLIDARITYNODE_SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true, always with APP_ENV=production: the settings, and so make check-config and every start, refuse production without it); only its SHA-256 is stored; lifetime SOLIDARITYNODE_SESSION_HOURS. Disabling a user or changing a password ends their sessions.
  • Roles for v0.1: viewer (shared scenarios and their results), analyst (also creates, edits, runs and shares own scenarios), admin (also manages users and imports data packages). Every endpoint that reads or writes scenarios, runs, results, users or packages checks them.
  • What "private" means. A private scenario, with its runs and results, is hidden from other analysts and from viewers, not from administrators: admins see, open, edit and run every scenario. This is deliberate. Admins operate the installation and have database access anyway, so hiding scenarios from them in the UI would only suggest a protection that does not exist. The UI says so: next to the visibility choice the analyst reads "Private: visible to you and to administrators", and an admin's Scenarios page lists other users' private scenarios in their own table, each labelled "private (owner X)". Tests: test_private_means_hidden_from_other_analysts_and_viewers_not_admins and test_opening_runs_per_role (backend).
  • At least one active admin. Admins cannot demote or disable themselves, and the last active admin can never be demoted or disabled; the check locks the admin rows, so two admins demoting each other at the same moment cannot leave none.
  • make create-admin creates the first administrator interactively. Two demo accounts are seeded only when APP_ENV=development (docs/uat/README.md).

Why: no extra container or identity component; enough for one installation on 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Facility staff and hub operator roles are not implemented (ticket entry waits for ADR 0010).
  • Throttling state lives in PostgreSQL, so it holds across API processes; a distributed attack from many addresses is limited only per username.

docs.title: Before the first pilot (not implemented now)
docs.text:
• Email invitations and password reset, with a forced password change at first sign-in (no admin ever knows a user's working password).
  • MFA with TOTP (authenticator apps), at least for admins.
  • Audit log of sign-ins (successful and failed), user changes, package imports and rollbacks, and exports: who, what, when, from which address; kept per OQ-21-compatible retention.
  • Provider support account: an account for the service provider that is disabled by default, enabled by the municipality for a limited time, and fully audited.
  • Transfer of ownership of a departing user's scenarios to another analyst, so disabling a user does not orphan shared work.
  • Onboarding guide for the municipal admin: first admin, users and roles, package import and rollback, backups (ADR 0008), what the throttling and lock messages mean.

docs.title: Later
docs.text:
• Single sign-on with OpenID Connect behind the existing IdentityProvider interface.
  • A facility manager role scoped to one facility (Paper 4: operational data per facility).
  • Per-facility device keys for ticket entry on shared devices without personal accounts, designed together with ADR 0010 and OQ-21 (no ticket is stored until those are decided).

docs.title: 0016. Scenario schema and versioning
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-24 (accepted for v0.1: 2026-11-25)
  • Related: Spec 00 §3 (Scenario), Paper 1 §13, Paper 3 §7–10, OQ-16, OQ-24; ADR 0003, 0013, 0017

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Spec 00 §3: a scenario is a set of changes relative to the baseline (an overlay, never a copy of the data): what-if interventions (Paper 1 §13, for example capacity +20 %, new facility) and disruptions (Paper 3: facility severities DS ∈ [0,1], closed network edges), plus a rationing case (OQ-24) and a reference-scenario flag (OQ-16). Scenarios are stored as versioned, schema-validated JSON with an owner and visibility (private, shared). core.model.Scenario already holds the typed form, with CapacityChange and NewFacility as placeholders without behaviour.

The demo scenario data/synthetic/demo/scenarios/C-DEMO-REF.json uses a draft layout (schema: "solidaritynode-scenario/0.1-draft"): id, version, name, kind, description, facility_severities, network_disruption (modes, affected_link_ids), interventions, rationing, reference_level. This is not a decision.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. JSON Schema published in the repo, generated from Pydantic models in the backend and mapped to core.model.Scenario.
  2. Pydantic models only (schema implied by code).
  3. YAML for authoring, JSON for storage.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Versioning: is every edit a new immutable version (needed for run reproducibility, ADR 0017)? How are versions numbered?
  • How does a scenario refer to features: stable ids from the data package (ADR 0013)? What happens when a referenced feature is closed in a newer package?
  • Schema evolution and migration of stored scenarios.
  • How the OQ-16 reference scenarios (minor, moderate, severe) are constructed: open, not part of this ADR.
  • Whether interventions and disruptions may be combined in one scenario (the spec does not say).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited: option 1, a Pydantic model with a published JSON Schema.

  • ScenarioBody (schema_version: "1.0"): capacity_changes (facility, service, input places | staff | throughput, absolute | relative percent, amount), new_facilities (id, name, type, an existing network node_id, services with capacity inputs), severities (DS ∈ [0, 1] per facility), closed_edges (edge_ids and modes), rationing (uniform | concentrated, required for disruption scenarios, OQ-24) and reference_level (the reference-scenario flag; construction of reference scenarios stays open, OQ-16). Unknown fields are refused. It maps to core.model.Scenario (NewFacility gains node_id).
  • Intervention placeholders (Paper 1 §13, §15.7), added without a schema version change because no scenario has been stored outside development (schema_version stays 1.0; the new fields default to empty, so stored versions stay valid):
  • network_changes.edge_changes: travel time or speed of one existing edge for one mode, absolute (minutes or km/h) or relative (percent, above −100 %);
  • network_changes.new_edges: a new edge between two existing nodes, with a travel time per mode and a closable flag;
  • population_changes: one unit and group, absolute (persons) or relative (percent). They map to core.model.EdgeChange, NewEdge and PopulationChange, are validated (schema rules, duplicates, references against the data version, no negative results where the baseline is known) and recorded only: runs list them under recorded_only (shown on the run page as "Recorded, no effect yet"), nothing is applied yet. The editor keeps them when saving and says they have no effect yet. Travel times and speeds must stay strictly positive (relative changes above −100 %, absolute travel-time changes leaving more than 0 minutes, new-edge times > 0): closing a road uses closed_edges, never a change to zero. A new edge that the same scenario also closes is reported on the run ("added, then closed, so no net effect", OQ-30), never ignored silently.
  • Order of application (OQ-30, proposed default, recorded in core.scenarios.overlay and core.model.Scenario): interventions first (new facilities, capacity, network, population), then disruptions (severities, closed edges), which may also hit the new facilities and new edges of the same scenario. This touches the method and must be confirmed when the Paper 3 spec is written.
  • The JSON Schema is exported to docs/schemas/scenario.schema.json (make schemas); a test keeps it current.
  • Scenarios refer to features by stable ids from the data package. Name, description and visibility (private | shared) belong to the scenario; every edit creates a new immutable numbered version (1, 2, …) that records the data version it was created against. Runs refer to versions, so old versions stay readable.
  • When a newer package closes or lacks a referenced feature, the scenario is reported (list, editor, import outcome) and cannot be run on that version until edited; nothing is dropped.
  • Delete is soft; a hard delete is refused when runs exist. Interventions and disruptions may be combined (the spec does not forbid it).

Maintainer decision (2026-11-25, PR #6): the optional core.model.NewFacility.node_id (the existing network node where a new facility is placed) is accepted.

Why: one source of truth for validation in the backend; the published schema lets the hub and other tools check scenarios.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A schema 2.0 will need a migration of stored versions.
  • Severities are recorded and reported only: how DS changes capacity is Paper 3 and not implemented. The same holds for edge, new-edge and population changes (Paper 1 §5, §6).
  • Open for later versions of the schema:
  • uncertain scenario parameters, for example DS as a range or distribution sampled in the Monte Carlo runs instead of a single value;
  • time-varying disruptions for Paper 4 (severities and closures that change over time), likely schema 2.0;
  • per-service severity (a facility disrupted for one service and not another);
  • scenario families for sensitivity analysis and for the OQ-16 reference scenarios (minor, moderate, severe), generated from one definition instead of edited one by one.

docs.title: 0017. Run reproducibility and result storage
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-24 (accepted for v0.1: 2026-11-25)
  • Related: Spec 00 §3 (Run, Result), AGENTS.md invariant 6 (uncertainty); ADR 0006, 0008, 0013, 0016

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Spec 00 §3: a run is one immutable execution of a scenario and records everything needed to reproduce it: scenario version, data package version, code version (git commit), model and parameter version (CPTs, priors), random seed, configuration. Lifecycle queued → running → succeeded | failed | cancelled, with progress. Identical inputs may reuse results. A result belongs to one run: summary values per unit × group × service (probabilities, intervals) in the database for maps; full Monte Carlo samples in Parquet files. Randomness goes through an explicit seed (AGENTS.md). /version already reports the git commit of the running build.

docs.title: Options to evaluate
docs.text:
1. Run record in PostgreSQL (inputs as foreign keys and hashes, lifecycle, progress) plus Parquet files per run in a content-addressed store; the database indexes them (ADR 0008).
  2. Experiment-tracking tool (for example MLflow, Apache-2.0) for run metadata and artefacts.
  3. Files only (run directory with run.json and Parquet), indexed by the database later.

docs.title: Questions to answer before deciding
docs.text:
• Exact fingerprint of a run (which inputs are hashed) and when results may be reused.
  • How the code version is pinned when the working tree is dirty (refuse to run outside development?).
  • Retention and deletion of samples; size limits; backup.
  • Model and parameter versioning for CPTs and priors (with ADR 0004, OQ-27).
  • How background jobs report progress and cancellation (ADR 0006).

docs.title: Answers for v0.1
docs.text:
• Fingerprint and reuse: the input hash below; a match is reused only when its results file is present and passes its SHA-256 check (see "Cached reuse").
  • Dirty or unknown code: refused in production; allowed in development with a visible warning (see "Code version").
  • Retention, size, backup: no automatic deletion of samples in v0.1; the size of each run's samples file is estimated before it starts (ADR 0008) and the Admin screen shows the results disk usage (samples files, runs, free space; GET /storage). The database and the results volume must be backed up together, at the same point in time, because run rows point to files and record their checksums: a note for the future backup guide (production operations ADR, see ADR 0012).
  • Parameter versions: open until models have CPTs and priors (ADR 0004, OQ-27).
  • Progress and cancellation: ADR 0006.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited: option 1, run record in PostgreSQL plus Parquet files.

  • A run is immutable and records: scenario id and version, data package id and version (and the data version row), code version (GIT_COMMIT of the build), model id and version (from the core model registry), random seed and configuration. Lifecycle, progress and error live in its job (ADR 0006).
  • Input hash: SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of scenario id, version and body, package id, version and manifest checksum, code version, model id and version, seed and configuration (no timestamps). Starting a run whose hash matches a succeeded run returns that run unless the user forces a rerun; failed or cancelled runs are never reused.
  • Code version. With APP_ENV=production, backend and worker refuse to start when GIT_COMMIT is unknown or ends in -dirty (settings validation, so make check-config fails too). In development such runs are allowed and carry a visible warning on the run page (code_version_dirty): they are reproducible only on the machine that made them. A worker built from a different commit (or with another model version) refuses a run queued for another one; the run fails with "This run was queued for code …, but the platform now runs code … Start the run again." Starting it again records the new code version.
  • Seed and draws. When a run is started without a seed, one is drawn (secrets, [0, 2^31)) and recorded (seed_source: drawn); the number of draws is recorded in the configuration (n_samples). The screens always send a seed (default 1), and the baseline run of an import uses seed 1, so their reuse is unchanged. Python, NumPy and platform versions of the worker are recorded on the run and in metadata.json (environment), not in the hash.
  • Cached reuse. Among succeeded runs with the same hash (newest first), the first whose samples file is present and passes its SHA-256 check is reused. If none passes, the new run records why (reuse_refused, shown on the run page) and computes the results again; from then on it is the run that is reused.
  • Result summary schema. Every result value (run_results, per unit × group × service × time × indicator) stores its mean, its median and two interval quantiles (low, high). The quantile levels are configurable (SOLIDARITYNODE_RESULT_INTERVAL_QUANTILES, default 0.05,0.95, a 90 % interval, 0 < low < 0.5 < high < 1), recorded in the run configuration as interval_quantiles and therefore part of the input hash. The statistics are computed from the model's samples by solidaritynode_core.uncertainty.summarise_result (linear interpolation); deterministic values have mean = median = low = high. A non-deterministic indicator without samples is refused. The per-sample values stay in Parquet (ADR 0008).
  • diagnostic-v0 was not changed by this summary schema (its version stayed 0.1.0; it became 0.2.0 later for joint draws, ADR 0008): its mean and its own 5 %/95 % bounds equal the stored mean and default quantiles, and the median is computed from its existing samples (core test test_diagnostic_summary_matches_its_samples_…).
  • Totals across units or groups are computed from the stored samples, draw by draw (summarise_total: draw i of the total is the sum of draw i of each part), then summarised. Medians and interval bounds are never added. No screen shows totals yet; any that is added must use this.
  • Comparison differences are differences of medians; the two intervals are shown next to them, not combined.
  • Export: CSV and GeoPackage columns median, low, high, mean; metadata.json states the quantile levels and what each column is.
  • Runs stored before migration 0005: value became mean; deterministic rows got median = mean; sampled rows have no median ("not available") and no recorded levels, because runs are immutable and their samples are not re-read. Start such a run again to get them.
  • Results: see ADR 0008 (samples are joint draws; the file's SHA-256 is recorded on the run and verified on read and export). Comparison is allowed between runs on the same data version (default: the baseline run created on import) or between two runs of the same scenario on different data versions (labelled); otherwise it is refused. Export: CSV or GeoPackage zipped with metadata.json holding every reproducibility field.
  • The only registered model is diagnostic-v0, which is labelled everywhere as "Diagnostic model: not a research result".

Why: run metadata stays queryable next to scenarios and data versions; files hold the bulk.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A dirty working tree gives a -dirty commit; such runs are reproducible only on that machine (development only).
  • Parameter versions (CPTs, priors) will join the hash when models have them (ADR 0004, OQ-27).
  • The comparison shows a difference of medians (labelled so in the UI, the API field difference_of_medians and its description). There is no comparison export yet; the run export has no difference column.
  • Open, to apply with the first research model: the uncertainty of a difference should come from draw-by-draw differences when both runs share data version, seed and number of draws (common random numbers), as summarise_total does for totals; otherwise the screens show the two medians and both intervals, labelled, and no interval for the difference.

docs.title: Open for later (from UAT, no code now)
docs.text:
• Hash the scenario's content, not its identity. The input hash includes the scenario id and version, so a duplicated scenario, or a new version that only changes the name or description, runs again although its changes are identical. With slow research models, consider hashing only the scenario's changes (the overlay body): identical changes would then reuse an earlier result, while each run still records which scenario and version asked for it (one result, several requesting runs). To decide with the first research model.
  • Retention rule for large installations. v0.1 deletes nothing automatically. A later rule could delete the per-sample Parquet files of old runs while keeping their summary values (mean, median, interval) in the database. The ADR must then say what is lost: such runs can no longer be exported with samples, re-summarised with other quantiles, compared draw by draw, or verified against their SHA-256. They are reproducible only by running them again with the recorded code, data, model and seed, not from storage alone.
  • A "New run" button. Today a new run of unchanged inputs needs a different seed (or the API's force). A UI button that forces a new run with the same seed would make repeat runs explicit, without suggesting that the seed is a setting to tune.

docs.title: 0018. Documentation site: MkDocs Material, mike, Mermaid
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted for v0.1, to be revisited
  • Date: 2026-11-25
  • Related: AGENTS.md "Diagrams", "Maintaining these instructions"; mkdocs.yml, tools/docs/, .github/workflows/docs.yml

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The documentation lives in Markdown under docs/ and at the repository root, and must read well on GitHub. Users (municipal staff), testers, researchers and developers need one navigable site with search, the user guide per platform version, and diagrams that change with the code. Files must not move, because code, tests and AGENTS.md link to their paths. Generated content (indexes, dependency lists) must not be maintained by hand.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. MkDocs + Material for MkDocs + mike (BSD-2-Clause, MIT, BSD-3-Clause): Markdown as is, Mermaid through pymdownx.superfences, built-in search, versions on GitHub Pages with a selector. Material announces end of life on 2027-05-05 (critical fixes until then); its successor Zensical reads mkdocs.yml.
  2. Zensical: the successor, younger; versioning support and plugin equivalents to be checked.
  3. Sphinx + MyST (BSD, MIT): powerful, but heavier configuration and a different Markdown dialect for admonitions and cross-references.
  4. GitHub rendering only: no search, no versions, no navigation for non-developers.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: MkDocs with the Material theme, versioned with mike and published to GitHub Pages from a workflow; all diagrams are Mermaid code blocks. A small hook (tools/docs/hooks.py) adds CHANGELOG.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md to the site without copying them and rewrites links that leave docs/ to GitHub. The tooling is a locked uv environment in tools/docs/ and is licence-checked like the rest.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• make docs, make docs-build (--strict, run in CI with link checking by lychee).
  • Indexes (ADRs, specs, open-question counts) and the dependency report are generated by scripts and checked in CI.
  • Revisit before 2027-05: migrate to Zensical (or another maintained option) once it supports versioned sites; mkdocs.yml and the Markdown should carry over.

docs.title: NNNN. Title
docs.text:
• Status: Proposed
  • Date: YYYY-MM-DD
  • Deciders:
  • Related: OQ-n, ADR NNNN

docs.title: Context
docs.text: What problem are we solving, and what constraints apply (AGENTS.md invariants, licence, Podman/Docker, privacy)?

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Option A: pros, cons, licence.
  2. Option B: pros, cons, licence.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The chosen option, stated in one sentence.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: What becomes easier or harder; follow-up tickets; what would make us revisit this.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Describes platform version 0.1.0. Overview and trust boundaries: Architecture. Settings are described once, in the configuration table of CONTRIBUTING; this page only names which settings each component reads.

flowchart TB
    FE["frontend<br/>frontend/"] -->|HTTP /api| BE["backend<br/>backend/src/solidaritynode_backend"]
    BE --> CORE["core<br/>core/src/solidaritynode_core"]
    W["worker<br/>python -m solidaritynode_backend.worker"] --> CORE
    BE --> DB[("db")]
    W --> DB
