docs.title: Paper 1 (accessibility, capacity, service gap)
docs.text:
OQ-1 (indices, §5–8). T_ij uses i as origin and j as facility, but demand and supply (D_j^g, Supply_j^g) are indexed by j, as if j were the demand location. Paper 3 also reuses s for scenario. Define one consistent notation. Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Indices: i spatial unit, f facility, g population group, s service, m transport mode, c scenario, t time, l state of a discrete variable (for example in Σ_l P(X = l) …).
  • Placement: demand, supply and gap belong to the spatial unit i; travel time is T_if^{g,m}.
  • Symbols fixed by other decisions: k intensity (service units per person per period, OQ-24); p need prevalence and τ take-up (OQ-8); P(·) probability. "k-anonymity" is used only as a term in text, never as a symbol.
  • Rationale. Removes the i/j inconsistency of Paper 1 and the double use of s in Paper 3, and avoids collisions created by later decisions (k as intensity and as state index).

OQ-2 (capacity allocation, §7). C_ij^effective = C_i^functional × w(T_ij) and Supply_j^g = Σ_i C_ij^effective. A facility's full capacity is counted for every origin, so supply can exceed what the facility can deliver when several areas compete for it. The text does not give an allocation or competition mechanism. Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Decision. Use a two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) allocation. Each facility's functional capacity is shared among the spatial units (and groups) that can reach it, in proportion to their access-weighted demand. Groups compete for the same facility capacity. The shares a facility gives out sum to its capacity.
  • Rationale.
  • Removes the over-counting of supply in the original formula, so the Service Gap is not systematically underestimated.
  • Does not redistribute demand to alternative facilities after a capacity loss. This matches Paper 3, which explicitly excludes adaptive redistribution and alternative activation (reserved for Paper 4).
  • Makes no assumption about how people choose facilities beyond the access weight w(T).
  • Cheap enough to run inside Monte Carlo and easy to explain.
  • Known limitations.
  • Demand inflation: a unit inside several catchments has its full demand counted in each one.
  • A unit can be allocated more supply than its demand while surplus capacity could cover another unit.
  • Notes for future work (tracked as research-question issues, not implemented now):
  • N-2a: 3SFCA. Evaluate a three-step floating catchment area variant (for example Wan, Zou & Sternberg, 2012) that splits each unit's demand among facilities with selection probabilities to correct demand inflation. Compare against 2SFCA on synthetic and real data. Verify references before use.
  • N-2b: Constrained allocation (option C) for sensitivity analysis. Implement a capacity-constrained allocation (linear programming or capacity-constrained gravity model) with flows bounded by facility capacity and by unit demand. Use it only as an alternative model in sensitivity analysis ("how much would the Service Gap change under coordinated allocation?"), never as the baseline. It assumes a behaviour rule and perfect coordination, which understates the real gap, and it redistributes demand after disruptions, which Paper 3 excludes.
  • N-2c: Paper 4. Constrained allocation is a natural candidate for modelling redistribution and resource mobilisation in Paper 4, where redistribution is part of the resilience mechanism.
  • Spec impact. Paper 1 §7 formulas for effective capacity and supply must be rewritten to the 2SFCA form. The access weight w(T) remains open (OQ-3).

OQ-3 (access weight, §5). Functional form and parameters of w(T) (decay, cut-offs), and whether they differ by group and mode, are not specified. Status: open.

OQ-4 (service gap vs BBN, §8–9). Service Gap is defined by a deterministic formula, then discretised, and also appears as a BBN node. It is unclear whether the BBN reproduces the formula, refines it, or models something beyond it, and how thresholds, CPTs and Monte Carlo interact. Status: open.

OQ-5 (modes, §3.4–5). Accessibility is computed per mode, but supply and gap are per group. How modes combine for a group (mode shares, best mode, weighting) is not specified. Status: open.

OQ-6 (groups, §4). Group definitions and thresholds, demand rates and their sources are not fixed. Groups can overlap (for example an elderly person with low income), so summing groups may double count population and demand. Overlap handling is not specified. Also (added 2026-11-23): tickets record a social group; decide whether a ticket can carry several groups or a priority rule applies, consistently with how population and demand handle overlap. Status: open.

OQ-7 (BN engine and discretisation, §9–10). Discretisation of continuous inputs, CPT size for nodes with many parents, the elicitation protocol and the choice of inference engine are open. Decide through ADRs. Status: open.

docs.title: Paper 2 (hidden need)
docs.text:
OQ-8 (from probability to quantity, §12). P(HN = Low/Medium/High) must become ExpectedHiddenNeed in the same units as demand to compute ETN = EstimatedDemand + ExpectedHiddenNeed. The conversion is not defined. Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Goal stated by the author. The method must support statements of the form "X % of the group has need that is not visible", so hidden need is measured in people of the group, not as a share of estimated demand. (Rejected: hidden need as a share of estimated demand, because a group that barely appears in services would then also show almost no hidden need, which may be exactly where hidden need is largest.)
  • Decision ("need prevalence × non-take-up").
  • p_{i,g,s}: need prevalence, the share of the group that needs the service in the reference period.
  • τ_{i,g,s}: take-up, the share of people with need who express it, that is make a request, whether or not they are then served. 1 − τ is non-take-up: people with need who never make a request because they do not seek the service, cannot access it, are discouraged by cost, distance or expected waiting, or use alternatives (Paper 2 §1.1).
  • Separation of concepts (decided 2026-11-23): hidden need is need that is never expressed (Paper 2). Unmet expressed need (requests not fulfilled within the maximum acceptable waiting time, or expired) belongs to Service Gap (Paper 1) and Service Loss (Paper 3). Defining τ as "served" instead would make capacity shortages look like low take-up and count the same unmet need twice.
  • Visible need (people) = Population × p × τ. Hidden need (people) = Population × p × (1 − τ). Share of the group with hidden need = p × (1 − τ). Total need (people) = Population × p.
  • The Paper 2 BN has four parents: Social Susceptibility, need-based gap (OQ-10), access deterrence and alternatives outside the network (OQ-11). Its target node is interpreted as the level of non-take-up, with states defined as ranges of 1 − τ (for example Low 0–20 %, Medium 20–50 %, High 50–80 %; exact bounds to be set with experts).
  • Expected non-take-up is Σ P(state) × value, with values sampled within each range in Monte Carlo (not fixed midpoints), so results are reported with an interval, for example "7–17 % of the group (90 % interval) has hidden need".
  • In service units (OQ-24): ETN = Population × p × k; hidden need in units = Population × p × (1 − τ) × k.
  • Source of p. To be determined during the work: survey or administrative data if available (candidates to check: EU-SILC, EHIS, SHARE for older people; usually national or regional, not per ΤΚ), otherwise expert elicitation. p is an uncertain parameter, configured per group, service and, where data allow, area. Not hard-coded.
  • Meaning of Paper 1 demand. Paper 1's DemandRate is visible use under average conditions (typically a national or regional rate), not need prevalence. If a source gives prevalence, it feeds p. This must be stated explicitly in Paper 1 §6.
  • Use of observations (revised 2026-11-23; replaces an earlier consistency check).
  • Rejected: requiring "visible need Population × p × τ ≈ Paper 1 estimated demand". Paper 1 demand applies an average rate and is not a local observation, so local differences are exactly what the method should reveal; and enforcing equality would fix τ = D / (Population × p) arithmetically, leaving the BN nothing to estimate.
  • Decided:
    1. Aggregate calibration where aggregate administrative figures exist (for example people served in the whole municipality): the sum of visible need over all units should be close to them; local differences are allowed.
    2. Observed use as evidence: local administrative records now, tickets later (Paper 4), enter the BN as observations and update take-up by Bayesian parameter learning of P(non-take-up | parents), pooling information across units with similar characteristics. Same mechanism as OQ-16; weight of experts against data per OQ-27. Updating per cell (unit × group × service × period) is avoided because counts are small and privacy rules (OQ-21) restrict them.
    3. Paper 1 demand is kept only as a descriptive indicator: the ratio of visible need to D shows where local use departs from the average.
  • Identifiability (limitation to state in Paper 2): use data observe only the product p × τ × k (how many requests), not need and take-up separately. Hidden-need estimates therefore rest on independent information about p (surveys or experts). Mandatory sensitivity analysis of hidden need with respect to p.
  • Persons versus requests: anonymous tickets count requests, not people. A ticket field "first request in this period" (yes/no, no identifier) allows counting people without identifying them, which separates k from p × τ.
  • Completeness of recording: if some facilities or channels (phone, walk-in) are not recorded, observed use is too low, τ is underestimated and hidden need overestimated. Recording coverage is tracked per facility and period, and updating uses only data from facilities with full or known coverage.
  • Change over time: take-up changes when services change; learning the CPT parameters (not a fixed τ per unit) lets τ follow changes in its parents.
  • Rationale.
  • Answers the author's question directly and bounds hidden need by the population automatically.
  • Splits two different questions (how many need, how many do not reach the service), each easier for experts ("out of 100 older people who need care, in an area with low accessibility and few alternatives, how many do not receive it?") and each validated separately.
  • Builds on the established non-take-up literature and on possible survey data for prevalence.
  • Links to Paper 4: tickets count people who reach services, informing τ once p is known.
  • Simplifies OQ-10: total need is Population × p; the BN only splits it into visible and hidden.
  • Easy to implement: array multiplications plus the discrete BN already required.
  • Notes for future work (tracked as research-question issues):
  • N-8a: Intensity of hidden need. People with hidden need may need more service units than visible users (for example because need accumulates). Initially the same k is used for both; revisit with data.
  • N-8b: Small area estimation. If regional survey data on unmet need become available, downscale them to spatial units with small area estimation methods using unit covariates, as an independent validation of the Paper 2 BN.
  • N-8c: Direct validation of hidden need. Tickets never show hidden need, by definition. Plan a validation study with direct measurement: outreach in a sample of units (home visits or telephone survey counting people with need who never requested help) and referrals from other actors (doctors, social workers, parishes) of people unknown to the services.
  • Spec impact. Paper 2 §1.1, §2, §10, §12, §17, §19.2 (non-take-up interpretation, people-based outputs, interval reporting), Paper 1 §6 (meaning of DemandRate), Paper 3 §5 (ETN definition).

OQ-9 (susceptibility index, §6–7 vs Paper 3 §12). Paper 2 writes SS_{i,g}, Paper 3 writes SS_g. Is susceptibility group-level or unit-and-group-level? Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Decision: SS_{i,g,s}, per spatial unit, group and service.
  • Rationale. Indicators such as living alone or household composition vary spatially, and a group is not equally prone to unmet provision for every service (for example older people living alone are highly susceptible for home care, much less for employment services).
  • Consequences.
  • Indicators, or their weighting, may differ by service; experts define them per group and service. The rule of Paper 2 §7 still applies: an indicator used to define the group is never reused as susceptibility evidence.
  • More elicitation effort than a single susceptibility per group; to be organised in the elicitation protocol (with OQ-7).
  • Unit-level indicators may be unavailable at fine resolution or based on very small counts; their uncertainty enters Monte Carlo, and small area estimation may be needed (see N-8b).
  • Susceptibility still never depends on the service system (availability, accessibility, capacity), as Paper 2 §6.2 requires; spatial variation comes only from social characteristics.
  • Spec impact. Paper 2 §6–7 and Paper 3 §12, §17 (write SS_{i,g,s}).

OQ-10 (possible double counting, §4, §10 and Paper 3). Hidden Need is conditioned on Service Gap, which is derived from estimated demand; ETN then adds hidden need to demand, and Paper 3 uses ETN to compute Service Loss. Verify that information is not counted twice (Paper 3 already flags this for Need Pressure). Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Original problem resolved by OQ-8. Total need is Population × p × k and no longer contains Paper 1 estimated demand, so demand is no longer counted both directly in ETN and indirectly through Service Gap.
  • Remaining problem found: a loop. Paper 1 Service Gap is computed from estimated demand, which reflects visible use (p × τ). Using it as a parent of non-take-up means that a group with low take-up shows low demand, hence a small gap, hence the BN infers low non-take-up: the group with the most hidden need would appear to have the least.
  • Decision ("option A"). The parent of non-take-up in Paper 2 is a need-based gap: max(0, Population × p × k − Supply), the shortfall of supply (2SFCA, OQ-2) relative to total need, not relative to current users. It does not depend on τ, so the loop is broken. Paper 1's demand-based Service Gap is unchanged and keeps answering Paper 1's question.
  • Rationale. People are discouraged by full facilities and long waits relative to everyone who needs the service, not relative to those already using it.
  • Rejected. Supply per inhabitant as parent (ignores how many need the service); keeping Paper 1 Service Gap with sensitivity checks (leaves the loop in place).
  • Spec impact. Paper 2 §9.2 ("Service Gap from Paper 1, not recomputed") must be rewritten: Paper 2 reuses Paper 1 supply but compares it with total need.

OQ-11 (diagram vs formula, §8 vs §10). The Paper 2 diagram shows Social Susceptibility feeding Service Gap and Accessibility, while §10 gives P(HN | SS, SG, A, ALT) with all four as parents of Hidden Need, and §6 states susceptibility is independent of service gap and accessibility. Fix the edge set. Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Edge set. Four parents of the non-take-up node, no edges between them: Social Susceptibility, need-based gap (OQ-10), access deterrence, alternatives outside the network. The §8 diagram, where susceptibility feeds Service Gap and Accessibility, is corrected, since §6.2 defines susceptibility as independent of the service system.
  • Problem found. The need-based gap uses 2SFCA supply, which already includes accessibility (through w(T)) and all reachable facilities. With accessibility and alternatives defined as in Paper 2 §9.3–9.4 (travel time, number and capacity of alternative facilities), the same information would enter twice. The three parents would also be derived from the same facilities and network, so experts would be asked about combinations that hardly occur.
  • Decision ("option A"): non-overlapping definitions.
  • Need-based gap: how adequate the facility network is for everyone who needs the service. Already includes access and alternative facilities.
  • Access deterrence: accessibility only as a direct deterrent to seeking the service (for example travel time to the nearest facility offering it), a different mechanism from how much capacity reaches the unit.
  • Alternatives outside the network: only options not among the modelled facilities (private services, family, NGOs, parishes), matching Paper 2 §1.1 ("use alternative solutions"). Where no data exist, start from expert estimates.
  • Rejected. Keeping only susceptibility and the need-based gap: simpler (9 combinations) but loses the "too far to ask" and "covered elsewhere" mechanisms.
  • Still to address (with OQ-7). Four three-state parents give 81 CPT rows. Candidate techniques: intermediate nodes (for example combining access deterrence and outside alternatives) or parametric elicitation such as ranked nodes (Fenton et al.; verify reference). Elicitation should skip or flag implausible combinations.
  • Spec impact. Paper 2 §8 (diagram), §9.3–9.4 (definitions of accessibility and alternatives), §10.

docs.title: Paper 3 (disruption, vulnerability)
docs.text:
OQ-12 (baseline gap inside service loss, §14–15). PUN = max(0, ETN − AvailableService^D) and SL = PUN / ETN. Because baseline supply may already be below ETN, SL mixes the baseline gap with disruption-induced loss. Should loss be measured relative to baseline available service? Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Definitions. For unit i, group g, service s, scenario c:
  • AS⁰: available service without disruption (baseline); ASᴰ: available service under the scenario.
  • PUN⁰ = max(0, ETN − AS⁰): baseline gap, need already unmet before any disruption.
  • PUNᴰ = max(0, ETN − ASᴰ): unmet need under the scenario.
  • Decision.
  • Disruption loss is the counterfactual difference ΔPUN = PUNᴰ − PUN⁰ (equivalently, covered need without disruption minus covered need with it). It is always computed and stored in absolute units (see OQ-24).
  • Service Loss (BN evidence) is SL = (PUNᴰ − PUN⁰) / ETN ("option A"), in [0, 1], equal to 0 when nothing changes.
  • Baseline gap stays outside Service Loss. Its effect is examined through Need Pressure in sensitivity analysis, as Paper 3 §6 already specifies. It becomes an additional BN parent only if sensitivity shows it adds independent information, and only through an ADR.
  • Relative Service Loss SL′ = (PUNᴰ − PUN⁰) / min(ETN, AS⁰) ("option A′", share of the service the group was receiving that is lost) is computed and stored as a secondary indicator for maps and sensitivity analysis. It is not a BN node.
  • Rationale.
  • Each parent of Vulnerability measures only its own aspect: Group Exposure (how much of the group is affected), Service Loss (how much service the event removes), Social Susceptibility (how prone the group is). The pre-existing condition of the group belongs to susceptibility or Need Pressure, not to the loss.
  • Passes the logical check that a zero-severity scenario gives zero loss. With the paper's formula the baseline gap would leak into Vulnerability, contradicting Paper 3 §6, which excludes Need Pressure as a parent to avoid double counting.
  • Consistent with Paper 4: loss is measured against pre-event performance (as in the resilience literature, for example Bruneau et al., 2003), so ServiceLoss(t) starts at 0 and returns to 0 on full recovery.
  • Normalising by ETN keeps the paper's wording ("share of estimated need"), matches the logic of Group Exposure (share of the group), and is stable for small values.
  • Known limitation. SL understates the consequence for groups that already had very little coverage (for example AS⁰ 100 → 0 with ETN 800 gives SL = 0.125 while SL′ = 1.0). This is why SL′ is kept as a secondary indicator.
  • Expert elicitation note. Experts filling the Vulnerability CPT must be told that "Service Loss High" means "the disruption left a large additional share of the group's total need uncovered", not "the group lost most of what it was receiving".
  • Spec impact. Paper 3 §14–15 and §28 must be rewritten with these definitions.

OQ-13 (affected population, §11). How AffectedPopulation is derived from dependency and accessibility (Paper 1), disrupted facilities and the disrupted network is described only in outline. Catchment and dependency rules are not specified. Status: open.

OQ-14 (disrupted service function, §13). AvailableService^D = f(Capacity^D, Accessibility^D) is unspecified. Is it the Paper 1 supply formula with disrupted inputs? Status: open.

OQ-15 (vulnerability states and thresholds, §17, §21). The network uses Low / Medium / High, while the elicitation table contains "Very High". Discretisation thresholds for Group Exposure and Service Loss are not given. Status: partly decided (2026-11-23).

  • Decided: Vulnerability has three states, Low / Medium / High. "Very High" is removed from the elicitation table of Paper 3 §21.
  • Open: discretisation thresholds for Group Exposure and Service Loss (with OQ-7).

OQ-24 (unit of need and depth of loss; raised while deciding OQ-12). In what unit are need, capacity and loss measured, and how is the depth of loss per person described? Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Decision: unit of need ("people × intensity").
  • Need is described by two quantities: the number of people with need N_{i,g,s} in the reference period, and the intensity k_{g,s}, the service units one person needs in that period (visits, appointments or hours, defined per service).
  • Need in service units is N × k. Capacity, 2SFCA allocation, Service Gap, unmet need and Service Loss are computed in service units. People are recovered when needed.
  • Each service has its own unit. Quantities of different services are never summed, consistent with the unit of analysis, which includes the service.
  • k_{g,s} is an uncertain parameter sampled in Monte Carlo, like the demand rate. People with need are N = Population × p (OQ-8); Paper 1's demand rate is visible use, not need prevalence (corrected by OQ-8).
  • Severity weighting across services is not applied now (see N-24a).
  • Decision: depth of loss ("option B").
  • The BN keeps Service Loss in service units (OQ-12); depth per person is not a BN parent.
  • How shortage is spread among people (rationing) is a scenario parameter with two bounding cases: uniform (everyone receives proportionally less) and concentrated (some are fully served, others not at all).
  • Secondary indicators are computed and stored for both cases, following the Foster–Greer–Thorbecke family of poverty measures (Foster, Greer & Thorbecke, 1984; verify reference): breadth (share of people who lose any service), depth (mean loss of those affected) and severity (loss weighted towards those who lose most, for example squared per-person loss).
  • Results report how conclusions change between the two rationing cases.
  • In Paper 4 the actual rationing pattern is estimated from tickets (fulfilled, overdue, expired requests per person).
  • Rationale. Capacity data (places, staff, throughput) is naturally in service units, and intensity differs strongly between groups (for example several visits a month for the elderly against one for the unemployed), so counting only people would hide real differences. Counting only units would hide how many people are affected. Rationing is unknown without operational data, so it is bounded by scenarios rather than assumed.
  • Notes for future work (tracked as research-question issues):
  • N-24a: Severity weighting. Weight service units by criticality or time-sensitivity (for example medical against administrative). Candidate for Paper 4, where resource types already appear. Weights require expert justification.
  • N-24b: Breadth as BN parent ("option C"). Consider breadth as an extra parent of Vulnerability only if sensitivity analysis shows it matters. It enlarges the expert table and correlates with Group Exposure.
  • Spec impact. Paper 1 §6–8 (demand, capacity and gap expressed in service units with N and k), Paper 2 §12 (hidden need in the same units), Paper 3 §13–15 (loss in units, rationing scenarios, secondary indicators), Paper 4 §4.2, §9 (observed rationing from tickets).

OQ-25 (reference period). Need and capacity must be measured over the same period (for example week or month). The choice also relates to the DBN time step in Paper 4 (OQ-17). Status: open.

OQ-26 (delay versus loss). When does a late service count as lost? Status: approach decided (2026-11-23), values open.

  • Decision. Each service has a maximum acceptable waiting time. A request not fulfilled within it counts as unmet need. This matches the overdue and expired request indicators of Paper 4 §4.2.
  • Open. The threshold value per service, and whether it differs by group. To be set with domain experts and recorded per service in configuration, not in code.

docs.title: Paper 3 and Paper 4
docs.text:
OQ-16 (definition of vulnerability, Paper 3 §2, §17 vs Paper 4 §2.1, §10). Paper 3 infers V_{i,g,sc} (original notation) per scenario from exposure, service loss and susceptibility. Paper 4 defines vulnerability as a baseline predisposition from demographic and socioeconomic factors and baseline accessibility and capacity, independent of a scenario, and updates it from observations. Reconcile: is vulnerability per scenario, a baseline, or both? Status: decided (2026-11-23).

  • Problem found. In Paper 4, Expected Consequence combines Vulnerability with the functional state of the system. If Vulnerability is Paper 3's (which already contains the disruption through Group Exposure and Service Loss), the disruption is counted twice. If it is Paper 4's baseline predisposition, it largely duplicates Social Susceptibility (Paper 2) plus the baseline system (Paper 1).
  • Decision ("option D"): vulnerability is the relationship, not a number.
  • The vulnerability of a group is how a disruption is turned into consequences for that group, given its Social Susceptibility. In the BN it is the conditional relationship P(V | GE, SL, SS), that is the CPT of the Vulnerability node, by analogy with vulnerability or fragility curves in seismic engineering (damage as a function of intensity, not the damage of one event; verify literature, for example the HAZUS methodology, before citing).
  • Paper 3 builds the relationship (CPT initialised by expert elicitation) and evaluates it at scenarios. V_{i,g,s,c} means "vulnerability evaluated at scenario c". Paper 3 §2 is kept, with wording adjusted to say that the scenario value is an evaluation of the group's vulnerability relationship.
  • Paper 4 evaluates the same relationship at observed disruptions: tickets give the functional state, from which observed GE(t) and SL(t) are derived, and the relationship gives the Expected Consequence. The disruption enters once, through GE and SL, so there is no double counting.
  • Bayesian updating in Paper 4 updates the parameters of the relationship (the CPT probabilities), not a state: standard parameter learning in Bayesian networks with the expert-elicited CPT as prior (for example Dirichlet distributions per CPT row; Koller & Friedman, 2009). Paper 4's statement that vulnerability is not a static indicator holds: the relationship learns from real operation.
  • Paper 4 §2.1 inputs are not a separate vulnerability concept: demographic and socioeconomic factors enter through Social Susceptibility; baseline accessibility and capacity enter through the simulation that produces GE and SL, and through Need Pressure.
  • Vulnerability is not risk. Averaging vulnerability over scenarios weighted by their probability of occurrence gives risk, which is a separate output. Vulnerability results must never depend on which scenarios happen to be included in a run.
  • Rationale. Keeps Paper 3's definition almost unchanged, removes double counting in Paper 4, avoids overlap with Social Susceptibility, makes results independent of the chosen scenario set, and turns Paper 4's updating into standard, well-documented parameter learning. The earlier proposal (vulnerability as an average over scenarios) was rejected because it conflates vulnerability with risk and depends on the scenario set.
  • Additions agreed with this decision.
  • Maps at reference scenarios. Vulnerability is mapped at standardised reference scenarios (for example minor, moderate, severe disruption), so that areas and groups are compared at the same intensity. Risk maps are produced separately, only if disruption probabilities become available.
  • Weight of experts against data: new question OQ-27.
  • Observation node. Because Vulnerability is latent, Paper 4 needs a measurement node P(ObservedConsequence | V) stating what is observed for each vulnerability level. To be specified together with OQ-18.
  • Spec impact. Paper 3 §2 and §17 (wording), Paper 3 §25–26 (maps at reference scenarios), Paper 4 §2.1, §8, §10 and the diagram in §15 must be rewritten. The domain invariant 2 (now in the root AGENTS.md) is updated accordingly.

docs.title: Paper 4 (operations, dynamics, resilience)
docs.text:
OQ-17 (DBN structure, §5, §12). How facility functional state is derived from indicators (rules or learned), their thresholds, the time-slice length and the DBN topology (for example first-order Markov) are not specified. Status: open.

OQ-18 (observed consequence, §9). How observed group consequence is computed from tickets, and against which denominator. Tickets observe demand, not hidden need. Since OQ-16, this also includes the measurement node P(ObservedConsequence | V) that links the latent Vulnerability to what tickets show. Status: open.

OQ-19 (resilience estimation, §13). How the five trajectory indicators combine, how continuous trajectories map to P(Resilience), and the baseline reference level are open. The research description states that final selection and weighting of indicators is part of the research. Status: open.

OQ-20 (resource mobilisation, §6). Parameters, activation delays and capacity limits of volunteer and other additional resources are not specified, and Paper 3 explicitly excludes adaptive capacity. Status: open.

OQ-27 (weight of expert priors against observed data; raised with OQ-16). When the Vulnerability CPT is learned from observed disruptions, the expert-elicited CPT acts as a prior with an equivalent sample size: how many observed disruptions should it take to move the experts' judgement? Options include a fixed equivalent sample size per CPT row, elicited confidence per row, or hierarchical pooling across units and groups. Also open: how to handle the small number of real disruptions and the dependence between observations in the same disruption. Status: open.

OQ-21 (re-identification risk, §4.1). Tickets are anonymous, but spatial unit, group and timestamps together can identify people in small units. Decide minimum cell sizes (k-anonymity), retention and aggregation rules before collecting any real data. These rules also limit how finely observations can be used for learning (OQ-8, OQ-16). The ticket field "first request in this period" (OQ-8) must not become an identifier. Status: open.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
OQ-22 (terminology). "ΤΚ" (Local Community) versus a generic spatial unit; group names (Low-income, Economically vulnerable); language of identifiers and documentation. Status: open.

OQ-23 (Digital Twin wording). Paper 1's conclusion calls the result a "probabilistic baseline Digital Twin", while the research description says a Digital Twin is not assumed from the start. Keep wording consistent in README and docs. Status: open.

OQ-28 (study-area buffer and cross-border demand; raised 2026-11-24 with the deployment model). People near a municipal boundary use facilities in neighbouring municipalities, and neighbouring residents use facilities inside it. A municipal installation therefore needs its municipality plus a buffer of neighbouring units, facilities and network. Open: buffer definition (fixed distance, travel-time threshold, or whole neighbouring municipalities); whether demand from buffer units competes for capacity in the 2SFCA allocation (OQ-2) while results are reported only for the municipality's own units; and how edge effects are tested. Added: when a buffer municipality is not yet onboarded (for example facilities: missing), results near that boundary are biased; decide whether to report a warning only (current platform behaviour), widen uncertainty, or use open-data facility estimates for the buffer. Status: open.

OQ-29 (facility on anonymous tickets; raised 2026-11-24 in the bootstrap PR). Paper 4 §4.1 and the privacy rule list spatial unit, group, service and timestamps, but not the facility. Facility functional state (Paper 4 §5), facility operational output (§14) and recording coverage (OQ-8) are per facility, so they cannot be computed without it. Status: decided (2026-11-24).

  • Decision. Every ticket records the facility_id of the facility where the request is made or scheduled (in practice the facility that issues the QR or appointment).
  • Rationale. A facility is not personal data, and it is required for the facility layer of Paper 4. Without it, facility state would need a separate data source and recording coverage could not be measured.
  • Privacy constraint. The combination spatial unit × group × service × facility × time raises re-identification risk in small units. The facility field is subject to the rules decided in OQ-21 / ADR 0010 (minimum cell sizes, aggregation, retention); until those are decided, no ticket is stored (as today).
  • Spec impact. Paper 4 §4.1 (ticket fields), §5 and §14; the privacy rule in AGENTS.md (allowed ticket fields).

OQ-30 (order of applying interventions and disruptions in one scenario; raised 2026-11-25 with ADR 0016). A scenario may combine what-if interventions (Paper 1 §13, §15.7: new facilities, capacity, network and population changes) with disruptions (Paper 3 §7–10: facility severities DS_{f,c}, closed edges). The papers do not say in which order they apply, and the order changes results: a disruption can hit a new facility only if the facility exists first, and a relative capacity change gives a different value before or after a severity is applied. This touches the method, so it must be confirmed when the Paper 3 spec is written (and then recorded in paper-revisions.md). Status: proposed (2026-11-25).

  • Proposed default (used by the platform, core.scenarios.apply_overlay, ADR 0016): interventions first, in the order new facilities, capacity changes, network changes (edge changes, then new edges), population changes; then disruptions (severities, then closed edges), which may also hit the new facilities and new edges of the same scenario.
  • Rationale. A disruption acts on the system as it is after the planned interventions ("what if we add a centre, and then a flood closes the road to it?"); applying disruptions first would make it impossible to disrupt what an intervention adds.
  • Open. Whether some combinations should be refused; whether a severity applies to a facility's capacity before or after a capacity change to the same facility (only recorded today, no behaviour).

docs.title: Paper revision notes
docs.text: Working notes for writing the final versions of Papers 1–4. Each entry records what must change in the paper text, why, and the decision it comes from (OQ-n in open-questions.md, where the full reasoning and rejected options are kept). Update this file whenever a decision is taken. Entries are written so they can be turned directly into methods, discussion and limitations sections.

docs.title: Notation (OQ-1)
docs.text:
• Change in all papers: i spatial unit, f facility, g group, s service, m transport mode, c scenario, t time, l state of a discrete variable. Demand, supply and gap belong to the spatial unit i; travel time is T_if^{g,m}. Other symbols: k intensity, p need prevalence, τ take-up, P(·) probability.
  • Specifically: Paper 1 §5–8 replaces j (used both as facility and as demand location) with f and i; Paper 3 replaces s for scenario with c.
  • Suggestion for the papers: a shared notation table, identical in all four, in the methods section.

docs.title: Units of measurement (OQ-24)
docs.text:
• Change: state that need, capacity, supply, gap and loss are measured in service units per reference period (visits, appointments or hours, defined per service), and that need is people with need × intensity (N × k). Quantities of different services are never summed.
  • Why: capacity data (places, staff, throughput) is naturally in service units, and intensity differs strongly between groups; counting only people hides intensity, counting only units hides how many people are affected.
  • Methods text: introduce N, k and the reference period (open, OQ-25) in the data and notation section of Paper 1 and reuse them in Papers 2–4.
  • Limitation to discuss: severity differences between services are not weighted (N-24a).

docs.title: Delay counts as loss beyond a threshold (OQ-26)
docs.text:
• Change: each service has a maximum acceptable waiting time; a request not fulfilled within it counts as unmet need. Threshold values set with domain experts.
  • Where: Paper 4 §4.2 (overdue and expired requests), and the definition of unmet need in Papers 1 and 3.

docs.title: §6 Demand rate means visible use under average conditions (OQ-8)
docs.text:
• Change: define DemandRate explicitly as the share of the group that makes requests for the service under average conditions (typically a national or regional rate), not the share that needs it. Need prevalence is introduced in Paper 2.
  • Why: keeps Paper 1 consistent with the hidden-need decomposition of Paper 2. State that estimated demand applies an average rate and is therefore not a local observation of use.
  • Also: demand becomes N × k in service units (OQ-24).

docs.title: §8 Service Gap covers unmet expressed need only (OQ-8)
docs.text: • Change: state that the Service Gap concerns need that is expressed (requests) but not met; need that is never expressed is the subject of Paper 2. The two never overlap.

docs.title: §7 Capacity allocation by 2SFCA (OQ-2)
docs.text:
• Change: replace C_ij^effective = C_i^functional × w(T_ij) and Supply_j^g = Σ_i C_ij^effective with a two-step floating catchment area allocation: each facility's functional capacity is shared among the units and groups that reach it, in proportion to access-weighted demand; groups compete for the same capacity.
  • Why (methods/discussion): the original formula counts a facility's full capacity for every area that reaches it, so supply exceeds what the facility can deliver and the Service Gap is underestimated. 2SFCA conserves each facility's capacity, does not redistribute demand after a capacity loss (consistent with Paper 3, which excludes adaptive redistribution), makes no behavioural assumption beyond w(T), and is cheap enough for Monte Carlo.
  • Limitations to discuss: demand inflation when a unit lies in several catchments; a unit may receive more supply than its demand while capacity elsewhere is short.
  • Future work to mention: 3SFCA as a refinement (N-2a); capacity-constrained allocation as an alternative model in sensitivity analysis, noting it assumes coordinated allocation and understates the gap (N-2b).

docs.title: Open items affecting Paper 1
docs.text: • Access weight w(T) (OQ-3), relation of the deterministic gap to the BBN (OQ-4), combining transport modes (OQ-5), group definitions and overlap (OQ-6), discretisation and BN engine (OQ-7).

docs.title: §1.1, §2, §10, §12 Hidden need as non-take-up (OQ-8)
docs.text:
• Change: decompose need into need prevalence p (share of the group that needs the service) and take-up τ (share of those with need who express it by making a request, whether or not they are then served).
  • Change: define three non-overlapping kinds of need: hidden (never expressed; this paper), unmet expressed (requests not fulfilled; Service Gap in Paper 1, Service Loss in Paper 3) and met. Explain that defining take-up as "being served" would make capacity shortages look like hidden need and count the same unmet need twice. Hidden need in people = Population × p × (1 − τ); share of the group with hidden need = p × (1 − τ); total need = Population × p (in units × k).
  • Change: the BN target node is the level of non-take-up (1 − τ), with states as ranges (for example 0–20 %, 20–50 %, 50–80 %), with four parents: Social Susceptibility, need-based gap (OQ-10), access deterrence and alternatives outside the network (OQ-11).
  • Change: report hidden need as a share of the group with an interval from Monte Carlo, for example "7–17 % of the group (90 % interval)".
  • Why (methods/discussion): the research question is "what share of the group has need that is not visible"; defining hidden need relative to estimated demand would make it vanish for groups that barely appear in services, possibly where it is largest. The decomposition separates two questions experts can answer more reliably, bounds hidden need by the population, connects to the non-take-up literature and to survey data on need or unmet need, and lets observed use (administrative records, tickets) update take-up.
  • Expert elicitation text: phrase questions as frequencies, for example "out of 100 older people who need care, in an area with low accessibility and few alternatives, how many do not receive it?".
  • Learning from observations (methods): observed use (administrative records now, tickets in Paper 4) enters as evidence and updates the parameters of P(non-take-up | parents) by Bayesian parameter learning, pooling across units with similar characteristics, with the expert CPT as prior (same mechanism as the vulnerability relationship in Paper 3/4). Updating per unit is avoided because counts are small and privacy rules restrict them. Where aggregate administrative figures exist, total visible need is calibrated against them; local differences are allowed.
  • Why not a local consistency check (discussion): Paper 1 demand applies an average rate, so local departures of visible need from it are exactly what the method should reveal; enforcing equality would determine take-up arithmetically and make the BN redundant. The ratio of visible need to Paper 1 demand is shown only as a descriptive indicator of where local use departs from the average.
  • Limitations to state:
  • Identifiability: use data observe only how many requests are made (p × τ × k), not need and take-up separately; hidden-need estimates rest on independent information about p. Report sensitivity of hidden need to p.
  • Recording completeness: unrecorded requests (facilities or channels outside the system) would lower observed use, underestimate take-up and overestimate hidden need; only facilities with full or known recording coverage are used for learning.
  • Persons versus requests: anonymous tickets count requests; a "first request in this period" flag (no identifier) is used to count people.
  • Data: source of p to be determined (candidates to check: EU-SILC, EHIS, SHARE; usually national or regional), otherwise expert elicitation.
  • Future work to mention: intensity of hidden need may differ from visible use (N-8a); small area estimation of unmet need from surveys as independent validation (N-8b); a direct validation study through outreach (home visits or telephone survey in sample units) and referrals from other actors, since tickets by definition never show hidden need (N-8c).

docs.title: §6–7 Social Susceptibility per unit, group and service (OQ-9)
docs.text:
• Change: write SS_{i,g,s}. Indicators, or their weighting, may differ by service; group-definition variables are still never reused.
  • Why: social characteristics vary spatially, and a group is not equally prone to unmet provision for every service (for example older people living alone for home care versus employment services).
  • Limitation to state: unit-level indicators may be coarse or based on small counts; their uncertainty is propagated by Monte Carlo.

docs.title: §8–10 Parents of non-take-up without overlap (OQ-11)
docs.text:
• Change (§8 diagram): four parents with no edges between them; remove the arrows from Social Susceptibility to Service Gap and Accessibility, which contradict §6.2.
  • Change (§9.3): accessibility enters only as access deterrence, the burden of reaching the service that discourages seeking it (for example travel time to the nearest facility).
  • Change (§9.4): alternatives are only options outside the modelled facility network (private services, family, NGOs, parishes), matching §1.1. Alternative facilities inside the network are already part of the need-based gap.
  • Why (methods/discussion): the need-based gap uses 2SFCA supply, which already includes accessibility and all reachable facilities; defining accessibility and alternatives as in the original §9.3–9.4 would count the same information twice and confront experts with combinations that hardly occur. The two remaining mechanisms ("too far to ask", "covered elsewhere") are distinct from network adequacy.
  • Limitation to discuss: data on outside alternatives may be scarce; initial values from experts. CPT size (81 rows) is handled in the elicitation protocol (intermediate nodes or parametric methods, OQ-7).

docs.title: §9.2 Need-based gap replaces Paper 1 Service Gap as parent (OQ-10)
docs.text:
• Change: the parent of non-take-up is the need-based gap max(0, Population × p × k − Supply), using Paper 1 supply but comparing it with total need, instead of reusing Paper 1's demand-based Service Gap "not recomputed".
  • Why (methods/discussion): Paper 1 demand reflects visible use, which already contains take-up. Using its gap as a parent creates a loop: low take-up gives low demand, a small gap, and hence an inferred low non-take-up, so the group with the most hidden need would appear to have the least. People are discouraged by shortage relative to everyone who needs the service, not relative to current users.

docs.title: §4, §22 Total need formula
docs.text:
• Change: replace EstimatedTotalNeed = EstimatedDemand + ExpectedHiddenNeed with ETN = Population × p × k, explaining that the BN splits total need into visible and hidden parts.
  • Why: removes the dependence of total need on estimated demand and simplifies the double-counting concern (OQ-10).

docs.title: §2, §17 Vulnerability as a relationship (OQ-16)
docs.text:
• Change: define the vulnerability of a group as the relationship that turns a disruption into consequences for that group, given its social susceptibility, represented by the CPT P(V | GE, SL, SS). A value V_{i,g,s,c} is that relationship evaluated at scenario c.
  • Why (methods/discussion): a single vulnerability number depends on the chosen disruption intensity; the relationship does not. The framing parallels vulnerability and fragility curves in seismic engineering (verify literature, for example HAZUS, before citing). It also allows Paper 4 to use and learn the same relationship.
  • Add: a sentence distinguishing vulnerability from risk (vulnerability weighted by disruption probabilities), and stating that results do not depend on which scenarios are run.

docs.title: §14–15, §28 Service Loss measures only the disruption (OQ-12)
docs.text:
• Change: introduce the baseline gap PUN⁰ = max(0, ETN − AS⁰) and define disruption loss as ΔPUN = PUNᴰ − PUN⁰. Service Loss becomes SL = (PUNᴰ − PUN⁰) / ETN.
  • Change: add Relative Service Loss SL′ = (PUNᴰ − PUN⁰) / min(ETN, AS⁰) as a secondary indicator for maps and sensitivity, not a BN node.
  • Why (methods/discussion): with the original PUN / ETN, a scenario with zero severity still shows loss wherever a baseline gap exists, so the baseline gap leaks into Vulnerability, contradicting §6, which excludes Need Pressure as a parent to avoid double counting. The new definition gives zero loss when nothing happens, keeps each parent of Vulnerability measuring only its own aspect, and matches the resilience literature, where loss is measured against pre-event performance (Bruneau et al., 2003), so Paper 4's ServiceLoss(t) starts and ends at zero.
  • Worked example for the paper: ETN 800, AS⁰ 700 → ASᴰ 500: original 0.375, new SL 0.25, SL′ 0.286; and with no disruption (700 → 700): original 0.125, new 0.
  • Limitation to discuss: SL understates the consequence for groups with very low baseline coverage (AS⁰ 100 → 0 gives SL 0.125, SL′ 1.0); hence SL′ is reported.
  • Expert elicitation text: "Service Loss High" means that the disruption left a large additional share of the group's total need uncovered.
  • Keep §6 as is: Need Pressure remains outside the core BN and is examined in sensitivity analysis.

docs.title: §13–15 Depth of loss and rationing (OQ-24)
docs.text:
• Change: add rationing as a scenario parameter with two bounding cases, uniform (everyone receives proportionally less) and concentrated (some are fully served, others not at all), and report per-person loss indicators in the Foster–Greer–Thorbecke style (Foster, Greer & Thorbecke, 1984; verify): breadth, depth, severity. These are outputs, not BN parents.
  • Why: the same loss in service units can mean everyone losing a little or a few losing everything; without operational data the pattern is unknown, so it is bounded rather than assumed.
  • Future work to mention: breadth as a BN parent only if sensitivity shows it matters (N-24b).

docs.title: §12, §17, §21 Susceptibility index and vulnerability states (OQ-9, OQ-15)
docs.text:
• Change: write SS_{i,g,s} (from Paper 2) instead of SS_g.
  • Change: Vulnerability has three states (Low, Medium, High); remove "Very High" from the elicitation table in §21. Discretisation thresholds for Group Exposure and Service Loss remain to be set.

docs.title: §25–26 Maps at reference scenarios (OQ-16)
docs.text: • Change: present vulnerability maps at standardised reference scenarios (minor, moderate, severe) so areas and groups are compared at the same intensity. Risk maps only if disruption probabilities become available.

docs.title: Open items affecting Paper 3
docs.text: • Affected population and catchments (OQ-13), disrupted service function (OQ-14), states and thresholds (OQ-15).

docs.title: §2.1, §8, §10, §15 Vulnerability used and learned, not redefined (OQ-16)
docs.text:
• Change: remove the separate "baseline vulnerability" built from demographic, socioeconomic, accessibility and capacity factors. State that demographic and socioeconomic factors enter through Social Susceptibility, and baseline accessibility and capacity through the simulation producing Group Exposure and Service Loss.
  • Change (§8): Expected Group Consequence is Paper 3's vulnerability relationship evaluated at the observed GE(t) and SL(t) derived from tickets and the territorial functional state. The disruption enters once.
  • Change (§10): Bayesian updating learns the parameters of the relationship (CPT probabilities) from observed consequences, with the expert-elicited CPT as prior (for example Dirichlet per row; Koller & Friedman, 2009), instead of updating a vulnerability state.
  • Add: a measurement node P(ObservedConsequence | V) linking the latent vulnerability to what tickets show (with OQ-18).
  • Update the diagram in §15 accordingly.
  • Why (methods/discussion): combining a scenario-based vulnerability with the functional state would count the disruption twice; a scenario-free baseline vulnerability would duplicate Social Susceptibility. Parameter learning keeps the statement that vulnerability "is not a static indicator" while using a standard, well-documented method.
  • Open: weight of expert priors against data, small number of real disruptions, dependence between observations (OQ-27).

docs.title: §11–13 Trajectories start at zero (OQ-12)
docs.text: • Change: define ServiceLoss(t) with the Paper 3 definition (loss relative to pre-event performance), so trajectories start at zero and full recovery returns to zero.

docs.title: §4.2, §9 Rationing observed from tickets (OQ-24)
docs.text:
• Add: the actual rationing pattern (how shortage is spread among people) is estimated from tickets (fulfilled, overdue, expired requests per person), replacing the bounding cases of Paper 3.
  • Add: tickets inform take-up τ (Paper 2) once need prevalence p is known, through learning of the Paper 2 CPT parameters, using only facilities with full or known recording coverage.

docs.title: §4.1 Ticket fields (OQ-8, OQ-6, OQ-21, OQ-29)
docs.text:
• Add: the facility_id where the request is made or scheduled (OQ-29), needed for facility functional state (§5), operational output (§14) and recording coverage; state that it falls under the same privacy rules (minimum cell sizes, aggregation, retention).
  • Add: a "first request in this period" flag (yes/no, no identifier) so that people can be counted without being identified; a rule for tickets of people belonging to several groups (OQ-6); and recording coverage per facility and period.

docs.title: Future work to mention
docs.text: • Capacity-constrained allocation as a model of redistribution and resource mobilisation (N-2c); severity weighting by service (N-24a).

docs.title: Open items affecting Paper 4
docs.text: • DBN structure and time step (OQ-17, OQ-25), observed consequence (OQ-18), resilience estimation (OQ-19), resource mobilisation (OQ-20), privacy of tickets (OQ-21).

docs.title: Original paper texts
docs.text:
This directory stores the original texts of Papers 1–4 verbatim. They are the reference against which every spec and line of code is checked.

Paper Topic Source file Spec written from it 1 Accessibility and service capacity (to be added) ../01-accessibility-capacity.md 2 Hidden need (to be added) ../02-hidden-need.md 3 Vulnerability (to be added) ../03-vulnerability.md 4 Resilience (to be added) ../04-resilience.md

Rules:

  • Do not edit these texts. Corrections to the method are recorded in ../open-questions.md and ../paper-revisions.md, and applied to the per-paper specs, not here.
  • Store each paper as Markdown or plain text with its section numbering intact, so references such as Paper 1 §7 resolve.
  • Record the version or date of each text at the top of its file.
  • No personal or operational data, and no material whose licence forbids redistribution under this repository.

docs.title: User acceptance testing (UAT)
docs.text:
Every pull request is tested by hand by the maintainer before it is merged. This page explains how to get a clean, repeatable test environment. Each PR has its own checklist: the "How to test (UAT)" section of the PR, and for larger changes a file in this folder (for example 00-bootstrap.md).

Everything runs on your own machine and listens on 127.0.0.1 only. The database contains synthetic data only (data/synthetic/packages/).

New to the platform? docs/concepts.md explains in plain language what a data package, a scenario, a run and a data version are, and who does what.

docs.title: 1. One-time setup on a fresh machine (Windows with WSL2 and Podman)
docs.text:
1. Install WSL2 with Ubuntu (PowerShell as administrator: wsl --install -d Ubuntu), restart, and open the Ubuntu terminal. All commands below run there.
  2. Install the tools: 
    sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git make podman podman-compose python3
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh          # uv (Python)
curl -fsSL https://fnm.vercel.app/install | bash         # fnm (Node.js versions)
    Open a new terminal, then: 
    fnm install 26 && fnm default 26
curl -fsSL https://get.pnpm.io/install.sh | sh -          # pnpm
    Open a new terminal again so all tools are on PATH.
  3. Get the code: 
    git clone https://github.com/SolidarityNode/snode.git && cd snode
  4. Check the tools and install dependencies: make setup. If a tool is missing, the message names it. make setup also creates .env from .env.example; you do not need to edit it.

Docker works too: prefix commands with CONTAINER_ENGINE=docker COMPOSE="docker compose".

docs.title: 2. Testing a pull request
docs.text:
git fetch origin
git switch <branch-of-the-PR>      # shown at the top of the PR
git pull
make setup                          # dependencies may have changed
make uat

make uat asks you to type yes because it deletes the local database and starts from a clean state. It then builds and starts everything, applies database migrations, imports the synthetic demo data package 1.0.0 (which also runs the baseline), creates the demo accounts and prints the addresses to open:

What Address Frontend (the application) http://127.0.0.1:8080 Frontend health page http://127.0.0.1:8080/health Backend API documentation http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs Backend health http://127.0.0.1:8000/health Backend version http://127.0.0.1:8000/version

docs.title: Demo accounts (development only)
docs.text:
make uat and make seed create two accounts, only when APP_ENV=development (the default of .env). Their passwords are public on purpose; never use them outside your own machine.

Username Password Role Can demo-admin demo-admin-pass admin everything, plus users and data package import demo-analyst demo-analyst-pass analyst create, edit, run and share own scenarios

A viewer (sees shared scenarios and results only) is created by the admin during the checklist. For a real installation create the first administrator with make create-admin instead.

Which build am I testing? The footer of every page shows the backend version, the git commit and APP_ENV, plus the commit the frontend was built from. They must match the last commit of the PR (git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD). A -dirty suffix means the code on your machine has local changes.

Automated tests first. make lint test (unit and integration tests) is run by the author; the end-to-end test runs in CI (job e2e) and locally with make test-e2e. Check that every CI job of the PR is green before starting UAT.

Then follow the PR's "How to test (UAT)" steps. Checklists so far:

  • 00-bootstrap.md: the skeleton (partly superseded).
  • 01-platform.md: the platform mechanics (data packages, scenarios, runs, results, comparison, users).

docs.title: 3. Looking inside the database
docs.text:
make db-shell

opens psql in the database container. Useful commands:

Command Shows \dt tables SELECT id, package_id, version, active FROM data_versions; imported data package versions SELECT feature_id, properties->>'role' FROM data_features WHERE layer = 'spatial_units' AND data_version_id = 1; the 8 fictional spatial units SELECT r.id, j.status, j.progress, j.error FROM runs r JOIN jobs j ON j.id = r.job_id; runs and their status \q quit

The database is also reachable from desktop tools (for example QGIS or DBeaver) at 127.0.0.1:5432, with the user, password and database name from .env.

docs.title: 4. Logs and status
docs.text: Command Use make ps are the containers (db, backend, worker, frontend) running and healthy? make logs follow all logs (Ctrl+C to stop following) make wait wait until the backend is ready make check-config APP_ENV=production would the backend accept this configuration in production? Lists every problem at once (exit code 1), never secret values

docs.title: Sign-in locks
docs.text:
After repeated failed sign-ins a username is delayed, then locked for 15 minutes (ADR 0015). Behind rootless Podman the platform cannot see browser addresses, so only usernames are counted: one person's wrong username or password never locks out another username. To clear locks before they expire:

Command Effect make clear-login-locks USERNAME=demo-analyst clear the delay or lock of one username make clear-login-locks clear every username and address

docs.title: 5. Starting again
docs.text: Command Effect make down stop everything; the database is kept make stop SERVICE=backend stop one service, keep the others running make up start again with the same database make seed import demo package 1.0.0 and the demo accounts (safe to repeat) make import-package PKG=… validate, preview and import a data package (directory or archive) make stop SERVICE=worker stop the background worker (a running run fails with a clear message) make reset delete the database, start, migrate and seed (asks for yes; FORCE=1 skips the question) make uat reset, then up, then print the addresses

docs.title: 6. Reporting a problem
docs.text:
• About a PR: comment on the PR with the step number, what you expected, what you saw, a screenshot if useful, the build commit from the footer, and the relevant part of make logs. The maintainer adds the uat-failed label.
  • Anything else: open a Bug report issue.
  • Never paste real personal data, passwords or the contents of .env into issues or comments.

docs.title: UAT 00: Bootstrap
docs.text:
Manual acceptance test for the bootstrap PR (chore/bootstrap). It checks that the skeleton installs, starts, shows which build is running, loads the synthetic demo data and keeps its safety rules. No scientific results exist yet.

Superseded in part by 01-platform.md: since the platform PR there is no demo schema; make seed imports demo package 1.0.0 instead (steps about make seed and demo.* tables no longer apply).

Before you start, complete the one-time setup in README.md. Tick each step when the result matches. If a step does not match, stop and report it (step number, what you saw, build commit) as a comment on the PR.

docs.title: A. Install and automated checks
docs.text: # Do this Expected result OK 1 git fetch origin && git switch chore/bootstrap && git pull Your branch is up to date (or a fast-forward). ☐ 2 git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD and write the value down A 12-character commit id, for example d4ab3121a0b2. Called COMMIT below. ☐ 3 make setup Ends without Error. If .env did not exist: Created .env from .env.example. No WARNING about missing keys. ☐ 4 make lint test Ends without Error; the three test runs report passed (core, backend) and Tests … passed (frontend). ☐

docs.title: B. Start a clean environment
docs.text: # Do this Expected result OK 5 make uat, type yes when asked After a few minutes: seed: loaded synthetic demo dataset … with a row count per table (for example demo.spatial_units 8 rows), then UAT environment ready (build COMMIT…) and five addresses. ☐ 6 make ps Three containers db, backend, frontend, each Up … (healthy); ports start with 127.0.0.1:. ☐

docs.title: C. The application
docs.text: # Do this Expected result OK 7 Open http://127.0.0.1:8080 Page titled SolidarityNode with links Home and Health. ☐ 8 Look at the footer AGPL-3.0 · synthetic data only · backend 0.0.1 (COMMIT, development) · frontend COMMIT. Both commits equal COMMIT. ☐ 9 Click Health Backend status: ok (backend 0.0.1, core 0.0.1). ☐ 10 Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/health {"status":"ok"} ☐ 11 Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/version JSON with "git_commit":"COMMIT…" and "app_env":"development". ☐ 12 Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs Page SolidarityNode API listing GET /health, GET /health/ready, GET /version. ☐ 13 make down, then open http://127.0.0.1:8080/health The page does not load (the stack is stopped). ☐ 14 make up, wait for it to finish, then reload http://127.0.0.1:8080/health Backend status: ok again. ☐ 15 Stop the backend only: make stop SERVICE=backend, then reload the Health page An error message instead of Backend status: ok; the footer shows backend unavailable. Then make up, make wait, reload: ok again. ☐

docs.title: D. Synthetic demo data in the database
docs.text:
Open the database shell with make db-shell, then type each query (end with ;, press Enter).

# Do this Expected result OK 16 \dn Schemas include demo and public. ☐ 17 SELECT version_num FROM alembic_version; 0002 ☐ 18 SELECT unit_id, municipality_id, role FROM demo.spatial_units ORDER BY 1; 8 rows: A1–A6 with M-A and core; B1, B2 with M-B and buffer. ☐ 19 SELECT f.facility_id, m.municipality_id FROM demo.facilities f JOIN demo.municipalities m ON ST_Within(f.geom, m.geom) ORDER BY 1; F1, F2, F3 in M-A; F4 in M-B (the facility across the border). ☐ 20 SELECT DISTINCT ST_SRID(geom) FROM demo.spatial_units; 2100 ☐ 21 SELECT mode, travel_time_min FROM demo.hand_check_travel_times WHERE scenario_id = 'baseline' AND unit_id = 'A4' AND facility_id = 'F2' ORDER BY mode; car 15 and walk 90. Check by hand: 5 + 2 + 0.5 km at 2 and 12 min/km (see the demo README). ☐ 22 SELECT scenario_id, travel_time_min FROM demo.hand_check_travel_times WHERE mode = 'walk' AND unit_id = 'A1' AND facility_id = 'F2' ORDER BY 1; baseline 66 and C-DEMO-REF 78: closing edge E02 makes the trip longer. ☐ 23 SELECT body->'facility_severities', body->'network_disruption'->'affected_link_ids' FROM demo.scenarios; {"F1": 0.5} and ["E02"]. ☐ 24 \dt public.* Only alembic_version and spatial_ref_sys: nothing from the demo is in public. ☐ 25 \q Back at the normal prompt. ☐ 26 make seed (run it twice) Both runs print the same row counts (demo.spatial_units 8 rows, demo.hand_check_travel_times 128 rows). ☐

Optional: open data/synthetic/demo/demo.gpkg in QGIS. Expected: four layers (municipalities, spatial_units, unit_centroids, facilities) in EPSG:2100, a 4 × 8 km grid in open sea; F4 just east of the municipal boundary.

docs.title: E. Safety rules
docs.text: # Do this Expected result OK 27 make check-config APP_ENV=production Fails with placeholder secrets must be replaced before starting: database_url (password). The password is not printed. ☐ 28 make check-config configuration OK (APP_ENV=development) ☐ 29 make reset, then type no Aborted.; make ps still shows the three containers, and step 18 still returns 8 rows. ☐ 30 git status --short No changes listed (in particular .env and data/local/ never appear). ☐ 31 grep -n '"127.0.0.1:' compose.yaml Three port lines (database, backend, frontend), all starting with 127.0.0.1:. ☐

docs.title: F. Finish
docs.text:
# Do this Expected result OK 32 make down Containers stopped. The database is kept for next time; make uat starts from scratch again. ☐

If every step matches, tick "UAT passed by maintainer" in the PR.

docs.title: UAT 01: Platform mechanics
docs.text:
Manual acceptance test for the platform PR (feat/platform-mechanics). It checks that a user can, in the browser and with synthetic data only, look at the study area, create and save a scenario, run it in the background, follow it, see and export results, compare them with the baseline, import a new data package version and find everything again. No scientific method exists yet: every result comes from the diagnostic model and carries a banner saying so.

Before you start, complete the one-time setup in README.md. Tick each step when the result matches. If a step does not match, stop and report it (step number, what you saw, build commit from the footer) as a comment on the PR.

Screenshots of every screen, taken on the synthetic data while walking through this checklist, are in screenshots/01-platform/.

Two browsers help: use a normal window for the analyst and a private window for the administrator or viewer, so both stay logged in.

docs.title: A. Start from a clean state
docs.text: # Do Expected result ✓ 1 In the terminal: make setup, then make uat and type yes After a few minutes it prints "UAT environment ready", the address http://127.0.0.1:8080 and two demo accounts: demo-admin / demo-admin-pass and demo-analyst / demo-analyst-pass. ☐ 2 make ps Four containers are Up: db, backend, worker, frontend (db, backend and frontend say healthy). ☐ 2a make check-config APP_ENV=production No Python traceback. The first line is "configuration INVALID (APP_ENV=production): N problem(s)", then one line per problem, at least: the session cookie (SOLIDARITYNODE_SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true) and the placeholder secret ("database_url (password)"), plus the code version if your checkout has local changes. No password or other secret value is printed. The last line is make's "make: *** [Makefile:…: check-config] Error 1" (the check exited with code 1; make itself then exits with 2). make check-config without APP_ENV says "configuration OK (APP_ENV=development)". ☐

docs.title: B. Log in
docs.text: # Do Expected result ✓ 3 Open http://127.0.0.1:8080 The Log in page opens.
